topics.title: What is accounting? Identify, measure, record, communicate

learn.hook: Every single UPI payment at a college canteen leaves a trail. Accounting is the art of turning thousands of such trails into one clear story: did the canteen make money this year?
points: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information about an organisation to the people who need it for decisions.
Identifying: deciding which events are financial transactions worth recording. Buying stock is recorded; the owner's friendly chat with a customer is not.
Measuring: expressing every recorded event in money (₹). Only what can be measured in money enters the books.
Recording: writing transactions in date (chronological) order in books of original entry, then classifying them into accounts and summarising them into statements.
Communicating: presenting the summarised information (profit and loss account, balance sheet, reports) to users in a form they can understand and act on.

example.q: Arjun runs a mobile-repair shop. Today (i) he bought spare parts for ₹8,000, (ii) a new competitor opened next door, (iii) he paid shop rent ₹5,000. Which events enter his books, and at what value?
steps: Ask: does the event change the business's financial position and can it be measured in money?
(i) Purchase of spare parts: yes, measured at ₹8,000.
(ii) A competitor opening: important, but no money value changes hands, so it is not recorded.
example.answer: Events (i) and (iii) are recorded, ₹13,000 in all; event (ii) is not recorded.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways handles crores of rupees of ticket sales every day. Its accountants identify each sale, measure it in rupees, record it, and finally communicate the yearly results to Parliament and the public.

options: Only preparing tax returns for the government

quiz.mistake: Records the hiring of an employee as if it were a transaction

quiz.explain: Communicating means passing summarised information to users in the form of reports and financial statements.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the process ends once entries are recorded

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The resignation of a firm's best salesperson is not recorded in the books.
Reason (R): Accounting records only events that can be measured in money.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Losing a talented person may hurt the business, but it cannot be measured in rupees, so it is not recorded. R explains A exactly.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every important event must be recorded

quiz.q: Classifying and summarising are carried out mainly after which activity?
quiz.explain: Once transactions are recorded in the journal, they are classified into ledger accounts and summarised into statements.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'My aunt says accounting is just writing numbers in a notebook. Is that all? Teach me the full process!'

topics.title: Book-keeping, accounting and the information system

learn.hook: Book-keeping is like scoring every ball in a cricket match. Accounting is the analyst who studies the scorecard and tells the captain why the team lost.
points: Book-keeping is the recording stage: identifying, measuring, recording and classifying transactions. It is routine and largely clerical.
Accounting begins where book-keeping ends: it summarises, analyses and interprets the recorded data and communicates the results.
Book-keeping is the base of accounting; accounting has a wider scope and needs judgement.
Accounting works as an information system: inputs are transactions; processing is recording, classifying and summarising; outputs are financial statements and reports for decision makers.
Because it communicates the financial results of every kind of enterprise in a common form, accounting is called the language of business.

example.q: A shop's clerk writes all sales and purchases into books daily. At year-end, a chartered accountant reads the books and tells the owner that profit fell because of rising transport costs. Which part is book-keeping and which is accounting?
steps: The clerk's daily recording of transactions = book-keeping.
Analysing the books and explaining why profit fell = analysis and interpretation, which belongs to accounting.
Passing the conclusion to the owner = communicating, also accounting.
example.answer: The clerk does book-keeping; the accountant's analysis, interpretation and communication is accounting.

learn.reallife: At a start-up such as a Bengaluru food-delivery firm, software records thousands of orders (book-keeping), while the finance team analyses margins per city to decide where to expand (accounting as an information system).

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Analysis and interpretation need recorded data, which book-keeping provides; so book-keeping is the foundation.

options: Junior staff or clerks, often using accounting software
quiz.explain: Book-keeping is routine and clerical, so it is done by junior staff or software; analysis needs senior accountants.
quiz.mistake: Assumes routine recording must be done by top officials

options: Deletes them after the day ends
Sends them directly to customers as bills
quiz.explain: Processing turns raw transactions into organised, summarised data that can be reported.
quiz.mistake: Confuses processing with an unrelated business action

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'If a clerk records every sale, why do we still need an accountant? Aren't they the same?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The clerk records; the accountant analyses, interprets and tells users what it means.
teach.nudge: Nice! What does an accountant do with the records that a book-keeper does not?

topics.title: Users of accounting information

learn.hook: When a bank like SBI decides whether to lend ₹2 crore to a textile mill in Surat, its credit officer reads one thing first: the mill's financial statements.
points: Internal users work inside the business: owners (is my investment earning?), management (planning, control, decisions) and employees (job security, wages, bonus).
External users are outside the business: investors and potential investors, lenders and banks, suppliers and creditors, government and tax authorities, customers, researchers and the public.
Each user needs different information: lenders need repaying capacity and security; creditors need short-term liquidity; investors need profitability and growth.
Government and tax authorities use accounts to assess tax (income tax, GST) and to frame policy; researchers use them for studies.
Customers want to know that the business will keep supplying goods and honouring warranties.

example.q: Match the user to the information: (i) Punjab National Bank considering a loan, (ii) workers' union negotiating bonus, (iii) a supplier selling on 30-day credit.
steps: (i) A lender wants to know whether the firm can repay principal and pay interest: solvency and repaying capacity.
(ii) Employees want profitability, because bonus and job security depend on profits.
(iii) A trade creditor wants to know whether the firm can pay within a short period: liquidity.
example.answer: Bank: repaying capacity; union: profits for bonus; supplier: short-term liquidity.

learn.reallife: Before a company lists on the NSE or BSE, its audited accounts go into the offer document so that lakhs of retail investors can judge its profitability.

topics.title: Qualitative characteristics of accounting information

learn.hook: A weather forecast is useless if it arrives after the monsoon storm, or if it is wrong. Accounting information has the same test: is it reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable?
points: Reliability: information must be verifiable, faithfully represent what happened, and be free from error and bias. Independent persons using the same method should reach the same figures.
Relevance: information must reach users in time and help them make decisions; it should have predictive value (helps forecast) or feedback value (confirms or corrects earlier expectations).
Understandability: information must be presented clearly so that users with reasonable business knowledge can understand it.
Comparability: users should be able to compare a firm's results over different periods (inter-period) and with other firms (inter-firm). This needs consistent methods and a common format.
These four characteristics decide how useful accounting information is; missing even one reduces its value.

example.q: A firm changes its method of valuing stock every year without disclosure, so this year's profit cannot be compared with last year's. Which qualitative characteristic is hurt?
steps: Ask: can users compare results across periods?
Changing methods each year breaks inter-period comparison.
So comparability is lost (consistency of methods supports comparability).
example.answer: Comparability

learn.reallife: RBI asks all banks to publish results in a common format each quarter, so analysts can compare HDFC Bank with Bank of Baroda: comparability in action.

quiz.explain: They are reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability.

topics.title: Objectives, role and limitations of accounting

learn.hook: No shopkeeper can remember 10,000 transactions. Accounting is the business's memory, its profit meter and its health report, all rolled into one.
points: Objectives: (1) maintain systematic and complete records of transactions; (2) calculate profit or loss for a period by matching revenues and expenses; (3) show the financial position (assets and liabilities) through a balance sheet; (4) provide information to users for decisions.
Role: accounting is the language of business and a historical record of transactions in date order.
It also reflects current economic reality (how wealthy the business is now), works as an information system and is a service activity that serves decision makers.

Limitations: it ignores non-monetary facts (staff skill, reputation); it records items at historical cost and is affected by changes in price level; it relies on estimates (useful life, bad debts) and on personal judgement in choosing methods.

example.q: Rohan bought a building in 2005 for ₹40 lakh. Today it could sell for ₹2 crore, yet his balance sheet shows it at cost less depreciation. Which limitation of accounting does this show?
steps: The asset is recorded at historical cost, the price paid when acquired.
Its market value has risen because of price-level changes, but books do not show that.
So the balance sheet does not reflect current value.
example.answer: Historical cost and price-level changes make the balance sheet differ from current market values.

learn.reallife: An ISRO vendor in Bengaluru may have world-class engineers, but their talent never appears in the balance sheet, because accounting ignores non-monetary facts.

topics.title: Basic terms I: entity, transaction, assets, liabilities, capital

learn.hook: Every business, from a pani-puri stall to Reliance, sits on one simple balance: what it owns equals what it owes to outsiders plus what it owes to its owner.
points: Entity: an organisation with a separate identity, like a shop, firm or company. A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party.

Assets: economic resources owned or controlled by the business that will bring future benefit. Non-current assets are held for long-term use (land, building, machinery); current assets are converted to cash within one year or the operating cycle (cash, debtors, stock).

Liabilities: amounts the business owes to outsiders. Non-current liabilities are payable after more than a year (long-term loan); current liabilities are payable within a year (creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft).
Capital: amount invested by the owner. It is the owner's claim on the assets, so Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

example.q: Neha's boutique has cash ₹30,000, stock ₹70,000, furniture ₹50,000, creditors ₹40,000 and a 3-year bank loan ₹60,000. Find her capital.

learn.reallife: A Kochi spice exporter's warehouse (non-current asset), its stock of cardamom (current asset) and its loan from SIDBI (non-current liability) all appear in its balance sheet.

topics.title: Basic terms II: revenue, expense, expenditure, profit, gain, discount

learn.hook: A sweet shop sells ₹1,00,000 of laddoos in Diwali week, gets a 10% trade discount from its supplier and also sells an old fridge at a profit. Are all these 'profit'? Accounting says no.
points: Sales: amount from selling the goods or services the business deals in. Revenue: amounts from regular operations, including sales, commission, interest, rent and dividends received.

Expense: cost used up in earning revenue during the period (rent, wages, depreciation). Expenditure: spending of money or creating a liability; if benefit lasts beyond the year it is capital expenditure (machinery), if within the year it is revenue expenditure.

Profit: excess of revenues over expenses of a period. Gain: profit from incidental or irregular events, such as selling a fixed asset above book value. Loss: excess of expenses over revenue, or money lost without benefit (fire, theft).

Trade discount: reduction in the list price at the time of sale; it is not recorded in the books. Cash discount: allowed for prompt payment; it is recorded (discount allowed is a loss, discount received is a gain).
Net amount after trade discount = List price × (1 − rate). Cash discount is then calculated on this net amount.

example.q: Goods with list price ₹50,000 are sold at 10% trade discount and 2% cash discount for immediate payment. How much cash is received?

learn.reallife: During the Big Billion Days sale, an online seller offers lower prices on MRP (trade discount) and an extra 'instant bank discount' for paying immediately with a card (similar to a cash discount for prompt payment).

options: Expense is always cash; expenditure is always credit

quiz.explain: All expenses arise from expenditure, but not all expenditure becomes this year's expense.

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'My cousin got 10% off on MRP and 2% off for paying cash. Are both discounts written in the shop's books?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Trade discount is off the list price and never recorded; cash discount is for prompt payment and is recorded!
teach.nudge: Good! But which discount is recorded, and which one never appears in the books?

topics.title: Basic terms III: voucher, goods, purchases, stock, drawings, debtors, creditors

learn.hook: When a kirana owner takes a packet of tea home for the family, that tiny act has a name in accounting, and it reduces his capital.
points: Voucher: documentary evidence supporting a transaction, such as a cash memo, invoice, receipt or salary slip.
Goods: items the business buys and sells as its regular activity. Furniture is goods for a furniture dealer but an asset for a lawyer.

Purchases: goods bought for resale or for production, either for cash or on credit. Stock (inventory): goods unsold on a date. Opening stock is at the start of the period; closing stock is at the end.
Drawings: cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use. Drawings reduce capital.
Debtors: persons or entities who owe money to the business, usually from credit sales. Creditors: persons or entities to whom the business owes money, usually for credit purchases.

example.q: A cycle dealer starts the year with stock ₹40,000, buys cycles worth ₹1,60,000, and at year-end has stock worth ₹30,000. What is the cost of cycles sold?
steps: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.

learn.reallife: A Ludhiana hosiery wholesaler sells to hundreds of retailers on credit. Those retailers are its debtors, and the yarn mills it buys from on credit are its creditors.

games.title: Goods or asset?
items: Laptops for a laptop dealer
A laptop used by a lawyer
Cars for a car showroom
Delivery van of a grocery shop
Furniture for a furniture dealer
Furniture in a doctor's clinic

quiz.q: A furniture dealer buys tables to resell. For him, these tables are
quiz.explain: Items bought for resale in the regular course of business are goods for that business.
quiz.mistake: Classifies items by their nature (furniture) instead of their purpose

quiz.q: The owner withdraws goods costing ₹3,000 for personal use. This is
quiz.explain: Any cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use is drawings, which reduces capital.
quiz.mistake: Treats goods taken by the owner as a sale

quiz.q: A person to whom the business owes money for goods bought on credit is a
quiz.explain: Creditors are those to whom the business owes money.
quiz.mistake: Swaps debtors and creditors

quiz.q: Opening stock ₹25,000, purchases ₹1,75,000, closing stock ₹40,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
quiz.explain: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.
quiz.mistake: Adds closing stock instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: A firm's capital was ₹2,00,000. The owner withdrew ₹15,000 for personal use and the firm earned a profit of ₹35,000. What is the closing capital?
quiz.explain: Profit increases capital and drawings reduce it.
quiz.mistake: Adds drawings to capital

quiz.q: Which document is an example of a voucher?
options: A cash memo issued for a cash sale
A price list sent to customers
quiz.explain: A voucher is documentary evidence of a transaction that has taken place; a cash memo proves a cash sale.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any business document is a voucher

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Purchases include both cash and credit purchases of goods.
Reason (R): Purchases means buying only fixed assets for the business.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Purchases are goods bought for resale or production, whether for cash or on credit. Buying fixed assets is not 'purchases' in accounting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks buying furniture or machinery counts as purchases

quiz.q: Total credit sales ₹3,00,000; cash received from these customers ₹2,20,000. What is the amount of debtors at the end?
quiz.explain: Debtors are customers who still owe the business.
quiz.mistake: Takes cash received as the debtors balance

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'A shopkeeper took a box of biscuits home. He says it is drawings. Isn't drawing about pictures?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Drawings are cash or goods the owner takes for personal use, and they reduce capital. No crayons involved!
teach.nudge: Good! Who takes the goods, and for what use? What happens to capital then?

chapters.title: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting

topics.title: Why accounting needs a theory base: GAAP

learn.hook: Imagine every cricket umpire using his own rules for LBW. Scores would be meaningless. Accounts without common rules would be just as useless.
points: If each accountant used personal rules, statements of different firms, or of the same firm in different years, could not be compared or trusted. A common theory base makes accounts uniform, comparable and reliable.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are the rules and guidelines followed in recording and reporting business transactions.
GAAP are known by several names: concepts, conventions, postulates, assumptions and modifying principles.

GAAP are man-made. They evolve over time from experience, usage and reasoning, are accepted by professional bodies (like ICAI) and are shaped by law and regulation. They change when business needs change.

example.q: Two shoe companies value their closing stock differently and do not say so. An investor compares their profits. What problem arises, and what solves it?
steps: Different, undisclosed methods make profits non-comparable: a higher profit may come from the method, not from better performance.
Uniform rules, GAAP, applied consistently and disclosed, solve this.
Then inter-firm and inter-period comparisons become meaningful.
example.answer: Profits cannot be compared fairly; following GAAP brings uniformity and comparability.

learn.reallife: When SEBI requires every listed company on the NSE to prepare accounts on common principles, a retail investor in Patna can compare Infosys and Wipro on the same footing.

quiz.explain: GAAP are Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the common rules of accounting.

quiz.mistake: Thinks the theory base is meant to hide information

quiz.explain: Vouchers are documentary evidence; concepts, conventions, postulates and assumptions are names for principles.

quiz.mistake: Thinks principles are permanent natural laws

quiz.mistake: Believes principles once made can never change

options: Are located in the same city

options: Reliability and comparability of the statements
quiz.explain: Changing rules at will makes statements unreliable and impossible to compare across years.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rules affect only the figures, not their usefulness

quiz.q: Which body in India plays a major role in developing accounting principles and standards?
options: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)
quiz.explain: ICAI, through its Accounting Standards Board, formulates accounting standards in India.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the central bank sets accounting rules for all businesses

teach.ask: Gappu ruffles his feathers: 'Why can't each accountant just follow his own rules? He knows his business best!'
teach.praise: Tweet! GAAP give everyone the same rules, so accounts are uniform, comparable and reliable!
teach.nudge: Hmm, if every firm uses its own rules, can we compare two firms? What common rules do we need?

topics.title: Concepts I: business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period

learn.hook: When a café owner in Pune pays her child's school fees from the café's cash, the café's books must not call it a business expense. Why? Because, in accounting, the café is a separate person.
points: Business entity concept: the business is separate from its owner. Only business transactions are recorded; the owner's capital is treated as a liability of the business towards the owner.
Money measurement concept: only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. Limitation: the value of the rupee changes over time, yet ₹1 of 2005 and ₹1 of today are added as equal.

Going concern concept: the business is assumed to continue for a long time, with no intention to close down. That is why fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation, not at their sale value, and assets are classified as current and non-current.

Accounting period concept: life of a business is divided into fixed periods, usually one year, to measure results. In India the financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March; listed companies also report quarterly (interim) results.

example.q: Mr Iyer brings ₹5,00,000 into his business and later pays his home electricity bill of ₹4,000 from business cash. How are these treated in the business books?
steps: Business entity concept: the business and Mr Iyer are separate.
₹5,00,000 brought in is capital, a liability of the business towards Mr Iyer.
Home electricity bill is a personal expense, so it is drawings, not a business expense.
example.answer: ₹5,00,000 is capital (owed to the owner); ₹4,000 is drawings.

learn.reallife: Every listed Indian company, from Maruti Suzuki to Asian Paints, announces quarterly results: the accounting period concept lets investors track performance without waiting for the company's life to end.

quiz.explain: Reputation cannot be measured in money, so it is not recorded.

quiz.mistake: Thinks any cash outflow is a business expense

quiz.q: Why do listed companies prepare quarterly results even though the financial year is twelve months?
options: Profit can be found only every three months
Quarterly results replace the balance sheet

quiz.explain: Interim reporting divides the life of the business into shorter periods to provide timely information.
quiz.mistake: Thinks quarterly results replace annual accounts

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'A shop is just its owner. If the owner buys a sofa for home with shop money, it's still the shop's sofa, right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The shop and the owner are separate. The home sofa is drawings, and capital is owed to the owner!
teach.nudge: Hmm, are the owner and the shop the same person in accounting? What do we call personal spending?

topics.title: Concepts II: cost, dual aspect and revenue recognition

learn.hook: A Jaipur jeweller buys a machine for ₹2,00,000, pays ₹10,000 freight and ₹15,000 for installation. Is the machine recorded at ₹2,00,000? The cost concept says no.
points: Cost concept: an asset is recorded at its acquisition cost, that is the price paid plus all costs to bring it to working condition (freight, cartage, installation). Later it is shown at cost less depreciation. Limitation: historical cost ignores price changes.
Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two equal effects. This gives the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital, which always holds.
Revenue recognition (realisation) concept: revenue is recognised when the right to receive it arises, i.e. when goods are sold or services rendered, not when cash is received.
Credit sales are therefore revenue on the date of sale; an advance received for goods to be delivered next year is not this year's revenue.

example.q: A machine is bought for ₹3,00,000, freight paid ₹12,000, installation ₹18,000. Five years later its market value is ₹4,50,000. At what cost is it recorded on purchase?
steps: Cost concept: include all costs to bring the asset into use.
The later market value of ₹4,50,000 is ignored.

learn.reallife: An airline like IndiGo sells tickets weeks in advance. Under revenue recognition it records the fare as revenue only when the flight actually flies; until then it is a liability.

items.q: Truck ₹8,00,000 + registration ₹40,000 + insurance for first year ₹20,000 (revenue). Truck cost?

items: Goods sold on credit in March 2026 are revenue of 2025-26, even if cash comes in April.
Revenue is recognised when the right to receive arises, at the sale.
An advance received in March for goods to be supplied in May is revenue of March.
The goods are not yet supplied, so revenue is not earned.
An asset's later market value is entered in the books under the cost concept.
Assets are recorded at acquisition cost, not market value.
Every transaction has two aspects of equal amount.
That is the dual aspect concept.
Installation charges of a new machine are added to its cost.
They are needed to bring the asset into working condition.

quiz.q: A machine is purchased for ₹4,50,000; carriage ₹20,000 and installation charges ₹30,000 are paid. At what amount is it recorded?
quiz.explain: All costs to bring the asset into working condition form part of its cost.
quiz.mistake: Records only the invoice price

quiz.q: The accounting equation is based on which concept?
quiz.explain: Every transaction affects two sides equally, so Assets always equal Liabilities + Capital.
quiz.mistake: Links the equation with going concern

quiz.q: Under the revenue recognition concept, revenue from a credit sale is recognised
options: On the date cash is received
At the end of the year only
On the date the goods are sold
When the customer places the order
quiz.explain: Revenue is recognised when the right to receive it arises, i.e. when the sale takes place.
quiz.mistake: Waits for cash to recognise revenue

quiz.explain: Capital = Assets − Liabilities.
quiz.mistake: Adds liabilities to assets

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Land bought for ₹50 lakh is still shown at ₹50 lakh though its market value is now ₹80 lakh.
Reason (R): Under the cost concept assets are recorded at acquisition cost.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The cost concept records assets at historical cost; land is not depreciated, so it stays at cost.
quiz.mistake: Believes assets are shown at market value

quiz.q: A firm receives ₹60,000 in March 2026 as advance for goods to be delivered in June 2026. For 2025-26 this amount is
options: A liability (advance from customer), not revenue
quiz.explain: Revenue arises only when goods are delivered; until then the firm owes the goods.
quiz.mistake: Treats every cash receipt as revenue

quiz.q: Which item is NOT included in the cost of a newly bought delivery van under the cost concept?
options: Fuel used on the van's daily delivery trips
Freight to bring it to the shop
quiz.explain: Running costs like fuel are revenue expenses; acquisition costs are capitalised.
quiz.mistake: Capitalises day-to-day running costs

quiz.q: Under the dual aspect concept, when goods of ₹25,000 are bought on credit,
options: Stock increases by ₹25,000 and creditors increase by ₹25,000
quiz.explain: An asset (stock) and a liability (creditors) both rise by the same amount.
quiz.mistake: Records only one effect of the transaction

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a customer pays in April for goods sold in March, when did the shop earn the money?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Revenue is earned when the sale happens and the right to receive arises, not when cash arrives!
teach.nudge: Close! Does revenue wait for cash? When does the right to receive money arise?

topics.title: Concepts III: matching, full disclosure and consistency

learn.hook: If you count Diwali-season sales in October but the salesmen's commission for those sales in December, October looks super-profitable and December looks terrible. The matching concept stops that illusion.
points: Matching concept: expenses of a period are matched with the revenues of the same period. Expenses incurred but not paid (outstanding) are added; expenses paid in advance (prepaid) are deducted.

Full disclosure concept: all material facts must be disclosed in the financial statements, including notes and footnotes, e.g. contingent liabilities, market value of investments, method of depreciation. Schedule III of the Companies Act lays down the format.
Consistency concept: the same accounting methods (stock valuation, depreciation) are followed year after year, so results are comparable.
Consistency does not forbid change. A method may change when the law or a standard requires it or it gives a better picture, but the change and its effect must be disclosed.

example.q: Salaries for March 2026, ₹40,000, were paid on 5 April 2026. In which year's profit and loss account is the expense shown?
steps: The salary was earned by staff in March 2026, which helped generate March's revenue.
Matching concept: show it in 2025-26, the year of the revenue.
On 31 March it is shown as outstanding salary, a current liability.
example.answer: In 2025-26, as outstanding salary of ₹40,000.

learn.reallife: Annual reports of companies like Larsen & Toubro carry pages of notes that explain contingent liabilities and accounting policies: the full disclosure concept at work.

quiz.explain: Material information that affects users' decisions must be disclosed, even if not yet a liability.

quiz.q: A firm uses the straight line method of depreciation one year and the written down value method the next, without any reason or disclosure. Which concept is violated?
quiz.explain: Consistency requires the same method to be followed from year to year.
quiz.mistake: Confuses consistency with conservatism

quiz.q: Insurance premium of ₹24,000 for 12 months is paid on 1 January 2026. Books close on 31 March 2026. How much is the expense for 2025-26?
quiz.explain: Only 3 months (January to March) relate to 2025-26; the remaining 9 months are prepaid.
quiz.mistake: Charges the whole premium to the year of payment

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A firm may change its method of stock valuation.
Reason (R): The consistency concept allows a change if it gives a better presentation, with disclosure of its effect.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Consistency is not rigid; justified changes are allowed but must be disclosed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks consistency forbids every change

quiz.q: Which schedule of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format of the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss, supporting full disclosure?
quiz.explain: Schedule III gives the format and disclosure requirements for company financial statements.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the old Schedule VI of the 1956 Act

quiz.q: Case: In 2025-26 a trader earned ₹5,00,000 revenue. Rent for the year is ₹60,000, of which ₹10,000 is still unpaid. What rent should be charged against this revenue?
quiz.explain: Matching charges the full rent of the year, paid or unpaid.
quiz.mistake: Charges only the rent actually paid

quiz.q: Which statement about the matching concept is correct?
options: It decides how assets are valued at market price
It decides who the owner of the business is
It requires all expenses to be paid in cash
It decides which expenses are charged against a period's revenue
quiz.explain: Matching links the expenses of a period with the revenue of that same period.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up matching with valuation

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'My uncle paid this year's last month of rent next year. Which year's rent is it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Matching charges it to the year it belongs to. Unpaid rent is shown as outstanding!
teach.nudge: Close! Does the year of payment decide it, or the year the rent relates to?

topics.title: Concepts IV: conservatism, materiality, objectivity and case spotting

learn.hook: A smart accountant is like a careful trekker in the Himalayas: count no summit before reaching it, but pack for every storm. That is conservatism.
points: Conservatism (prudence): anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses. Examples: closing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower; provision for doubtful debts.
Conservatism should not be overdone; deliberately understating profit creates secret reserves, which is not allowed.
Materiality: items significant enough to influence users' decisions must be disclosed separately; trivial items (a ₹50 stapler) may be treated as expenses even if they last for years.
Objectivity: transactions must be recorded on the basis of verifiable evidence (invoices, receipts), free from personal bias.

To identify a concept in a case, ask what rule the action follows: separation of owner, money value, continuity, period, cost, two effects, earning, matching, disclosure, sameness, caution, significance or evidence.

example.q: Closing stock cost ₹1,20,000; its market (realisable) value is ₹1,05,000. At what value is it shown, and why?
steps: Compare cost ₹1,20,000 and net realisable value ₹1,05,000.
Conservatism: take the lower, to provide for the expected loss.
example.answer: ₹1,05,000, under the conservatism concept.

learn.reallife: Banks regulated by RBI must set aside provisions for loans that may go bad, even before the borrower actually defaults: prudence written into rules.

topics.title: Systems of accounting: double entry and single entry

learn.hook: A big hospital like AIIMS records every rupee twice, once as a debit and once as a credit. A tiny tea stall may just keep a cash diary. Both are 'systems', but only one is complete.
points: Double entry system: both aspects (debit and credit) of every transaction are recorded. It is complete and scientific, its arithmetical accuracy can be checked by a trial balance, and it helps detect fraud.
It is used by companies and most organisations; it needs trained staff and is costlier.
Single entry system: an incomplete system in which mostly personal accounts (debtors, creditors) and the cash book are kept. Nominal and real accounts are usually not maintained.
Single entry is simple and cheap, so small traders use it, but no trial balance can be prepared, true profit is hard to find, and it is not reliable for tax or loans.

example.q: A small cloth trader keeps only a cash book and a list of customers who owe him. Can he prepare a trial balance? Which system is this?
steps: He records only cash and personal accounts.
Nominal and real accounts are missing, so debit and credit totals cannot be matched.
This is single entry (incomplete records); a trial balance cannot be prepared.
example.answer: No trial balance is possible; it is the single entry system.

learn.reallife: GST law and lenders such as MUDRA-scheme banks rely on proper books; many small traders in Indian bazaars move from a simple bahi-khata diary to double-entry accounting apps as they grow.

topics.title: Basis of accounting: cash basis vs accrual basis

learn.hook: A tuition centre in Kota collects fees for April in March. Under one basis, March looks rich. Under the other, the money is not yet earned. Which basis is right?
points: Cash basis: entries are made only when cash is received or paid. Income = cash received; expense = cash paid. Outstanding and prepaid items are ignored.
Accrual basis: revenues are recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. It follows the matching concept.
Companies must follow the accrual basis under the Companies Act, 2013. Cash basis suits small professionals and non-profit bodies with simple needs.
Profit under cash basis = Cash received from income − Cash paid for expenses. Profit under accrual basis = Income earned − Expenses incurred.

example.q: In 2025-26 a consultant earned fees of ₹6,00,000 but received only ₹5,20,000. Expenses incurred were ₹2,80,000, of which ₹2,50,000 was paid. Find profit under both bases.
steps: The difference arises from unreceived fees ₹80,000 and unpaid expenses ₹30,000.
example.answer: Cash basis ₹2,70,000; accrual basis ₹3,20,000.

learn.reallife: Government departments in India have traditionally used cash-based accounts, while companies listed on the BSE must use accrual accounting for a true picture of profit.

topics.title: Accounting standards, Ind AS and IFRS

learn.hook: Whether a company's accounts are read in Mumbai, London or Tokyo, investors want them written in the same 'grammar'. Accounting standards are that grammar.
points: Accounting standards are written policy documents issued by an expert body that cover the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions in financial statements.
In India, the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of the ICAI, set up in 1977, formulates standards; they become mandatory for companies when notified by the Central Government.
Benefits: uniformity in accounting, better inter-firm comparability, fewer alternative treatments, more disclosure and greater reliability.
Limitations: choosing between alternatives is hard, standards may be rigid, and they cannot override the law.

IFRS are global standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). India chose convergence, not direct adoption: Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) are converged with IFRS and apply in phases to listed and large companies (first phase from 1 April 2016).

example.q: An Indian software company with branches in 40 countries prepares accounts under Ind AS. Why does this help a foreign investor?
steps: Ind AS are converged with IFRS, the global standards.
So the company's statements are broadly comparable with those of foreign companies using IFRS.
The investor can compare without re-working the numbers.
example.answer: Global comparability, because Ind AS are converged with IFRS.

learn.reallife: When large Indian companies moved to Ind AS from 2016 onwards, foreign institutional investors found it easier to compare them with global peers.

topics.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST): basics and calculation

learn.hook: Before 1 July 2017, a truck carrying biscuits from Delhi to Chennai could face several different state taxes. GST replaced that tangle with 'one nation, one tax'.
points: GST is a comprehensive, destination-based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It came into force on 1 July 2017 and replaced many indirect taxes such as central excise duty (on most goods), VAT and service tax.
Intra-state supply (seller and buyer in the same state): CGST (to the Centre) + SGST (to the State), each at half the total rate. In union territories without a legislature, UTGST replaces SGST.
Inter-state supply (different states): IGST at the full rate, collected by the Centre.
Input tax credit (ITC): GST paid on purchases is set off against GST collected on sales, so tax is paid only on value added. This removes the cascading (tax-on-tax) effect.
Features and advantages: uniform rates and procedures, online compliance through the GST Network (GSTN), wider tax base, transparency and ease of doing business.

example.q: A Lucknow trader sells goods worth ₹50,000 (a) to a buyer in Kanpur, (b) to a buyer in Patna. GST rate is 18%. Compute the tax.
steps: Lucknow and Kanpur are both in Uttar Pradesh: intra-state. CGST 9% = ₹4,500 and SGST 9% = ₹4,500.
Total tax is ₹9,000 in both cases; only the components differ.

learn.reallife: GST invoices generated across India flow through the GST Network portal, so a dealer in Guwahati can claim input tax credit for tax his supplier in Surat has paid.

topics.title: Business transactions and source documents

learn.hook: Every entry in the books of a company like Amul begins with a piece of paper or a digital slip: a bill, a receipt, a cheque. No paper, no entry.
points: A business transaction is an exchange of economic value (money or money's worth) between the business and another party. Every transaction has a two-fold effect.
A source document is the written evidence of a transaction, prepared at the time it happens. It is the basis for recording.
Common source documents: cash memo (cash sale), invoice or bill (credit sale), receipt (cash received), pay-in-slip (cash or cheque deposited in bank), cheque (order to a bank to pay), salary slip.

Debit note: sent by the buyer to the seller when goods are returned, informing that the seller's account has been debited. Credit note: sent by the seller to the buyer for goods returned, informing that the buyer's account has been credited.

example.q: Riya returns damaged goods worth ₹4,000 to her supplier Mehta Traders. Which document does she send, and which does Mehta Traders send her?
steps: Riya, the buyer, returns goods and debits the supplier's account: she sends a debit note.
Mehta Traders, the seller, accepts the return and credits Riya's account: it sends a credit note.
example.answer: Riya sends a debit note; Mehta Traders sends a credit note.

learn.reallife: When you deposit cash at a bank branch, you fill a pay-in-slip; its counterfoil, stamped by the cashier, is the source document for your entry.

topics.title: Accounting vouchers: types and preparation

learn.hook: In a large firm, no accountant writes an entry from memory. A voucher, signed and numbered, travels with every transaction like a boarding pass.
points: An accounting voucher is prepared from source documents. It records the accounts to be debited and credited, and is authorised by a responsible person.
Contents: name of firm, voucher number, date, accounts debited and credited with amounts, narration (brief explanation), and signatures of the preparer and the authoriser.

Cash vouchers: debit voucher (for cash payment) and credit voucher (for cash receipt). Non-cash or transfer (journal) vouchers are used for transactions without cash, e.g. credit purchases or depreciation.
Transaction voucher: one debit and one credit. Compound voucher: one debit with several credits, or one credit with several debits. Complex voucher: several debits and several credits.

example.q: Rent ₹15,000 is paid in cash. Which voucher is prepared, and what does it show?
steps: Cash goes out, so a cash payment voucher, i.e. a debit voucher, is prepared.
Account debited: Rent A/c ₹15,000; account credited: Cash A/c ₹15,000.
Narration: 'Being rent paid for the month'; signed by the preparer and authorised by the manager.
example.answer: A debit voucher: Dr Rent ₹15,000 / Cr Cash ₹15,000.

learn.reallife: Government offices in India pass every payment through a numbered voucher signed by the drawing and disbursing officer, so auditors from the CAG can trace each rupee.

topics.title: The accounting equation: A = L + C

learn.hook: No matter what happens in a business, this equation never breaks: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Every transaction is like a see-saw that stays level.
points: Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Variants: Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital.
Every transaction changes at least two items so that the equation still balances.

Possible effects: both sides increase (goods bought on credit); both sides decrease (creditor paid); one asset up and another down (furniture bought for cash); one liability up and another down (creditor paid by a bill payable).
A tabular analysis lists each transaction with its effect on each asset, liability and capital; totals of both sides match after every line.

example.q: Start: cash ₹1,00,000 = capital ₹1,00,000. (1) Goods bought on credit ₹30,000. (2) Furniture bought for cash ₹20,000. Show the equation after both.
steps: (2) Furniture +20,000, cash −20,000: assets change between themselves.

learn.reallife: Even a startup in Bengaluru raising ₹10 crore from investors records it as cash up and capital up by the same ₹10 crore, keeping the equation balanced.

topics.title: Accounting equation: revenue, expenses, drawings and full numericals

learn.hook: Sell goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹14,000 and something magical happens in the equation: capital grows by exactly ₹4,000.
points: Revenue and profit increase capital; expenses, losses and drawings reduce capital.
Sale of goods at a profit: cash or debtors rise by the sale price, stock falls by the cost, and capital rises by the profit.
Expenses paid in cash (rent, salary): cash falls and capital falls. Outstanding expenses: liabilities rise and capital falls.
Drawings in cash or goods: assets fall and capital falls.
After a series of transactions, the final balances of the equation give the balance sheet.

example.q: Capital ₹1,00,000 in cash. (1) Bought goods ₹40,000 cash. (2) Sold goods costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 on credit. (3) Paid rent ₹5,000. (4) Withdrew ₹3,000 cash. Find the final capital.
steps: Check: cash 52,000 + stock 10,000 + debtors 45,000 = ₹1,07,000 = capital (no liabilities).

learn.reallife: A food-truck owner at Juhu beach sees capital rise with every profitable evening and fall every time she takes cash home: the equation tracks her real stake.

topics.title: Debit, credit and the rules for each type of account

learn.hook: Debit is not 'bad' and credit is not 'good'. In accounting, they simply mean left and right, like the two sides of a cricket pitch.
points: An account is a summarised record of all transactions about one item (Cash A/c, Rent A/c). A T-account has the debit side on the left and the credit side on the right.
Assets and expenses/losses: increase is debited, decrease is credited.
Liabilities, capital and revenues/gains: increase is credited, decrease is debited.
Drawings reduce capital, so drawings are debited.
To find the entry: identify the two accounts, decide each one's type, decide increase or decrease, and apply the rule.

example.q: Paid salary ₹20,000 by cheque. Which account is debited and which credited?
steps: Accounts affected: Salary A/c and Bank A/c.
Salary is an expense and it increases: debit Salary.
Bank is an asset and it decreases: credit Bank.
example.answer: Dr Salary ₹20,000 / Cr Bank ₹20,000

learn.reallife: When Indian Railways buys a new locomotive on credit, its accountants debit the Locomotive (asset increases) and credit the supplier (liability increases).

topics.title: Traditional classification and the golden rules

learn.hook: Long before computers, Indian munims kept the bahi-khata with three golden rules. They still give the same answers as the modern equation approach.
points: Traditional classification: personal accounts (persons, firms, companies, banks, capital, drawings); real accounts (assets such as cash, furniture, goodwill); nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains).
Personal account: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.
Capital and drawings are personal accounts of the owner. Outstanding and prepaid expense accounts are representative personal accounts.

example.q: Cash sales ₹15,000. Apply the golden rules.
steps: Sales is an income: credit Sales.
example.answer: Dr Cash ₹15,000 / Cr Sales ₹15,000

topics.title: The journal: format, simple and compound entries

learn.hook: The journal is the diary of a business: every transaction enters it first, date by date, before going anywhere else. That's why it's called the book of original entry.
points: Journal: the book of original (prime) entry where transactions are first recorded in chronological order. Recording in it is called journalising.
Format: Date | Particulars (debit account with 'Dr', credit account prefixed with 'To', then narration in brackets) | L.F. (ledger folio) | Debit amount (₹) | Credit amount (₹).
Simple entry: one debit and one credit. Compound entry: more than one debit or more than one credit, e.g. payment with discount.

Typical entries: Capital: Dr Cash / Cr Capital. Cash purchases: Dr Purchases / Cr Cash. Credit sales: Dr Debtor / Cr Sales. Purchases returned: Dr Creditor / Cr Purchases Return. Sales returned: Dr Sales Return / Cr Debtor.
Payment with discount: Dr Creditor (full amount) / Cr Cash (amount paid) / Cr Discount Received (discount).

example.q: Paid ₹19,600 to Sohan in full settlement of ₹20,000 owed to him. Journalise.
steps: Sohan's liability of ₹20,000 is fully cleared: debit Sohan ₹20,000.
Discount received = 20,000 − 19,600 = ₹400: credit Discount Received (a gain).
example.answer: Dr Sohan ₹20,000 / Cr Cash ₹19,600 / Cr Discount Received ₹400

learn.reallife: Every UPI transfer you make generates a dated record on the bank's server, the digital cousin of a journal entry.

topics.title: Special journal entries: drawings of goods, charity, samples, losses

learn.hook: A sweet shop gives free laddoos to customers as samples, donates boxes to an orphanage on Independence Day, and the owner takes some home for family. Each one is a different entry.
points: Goods taken by the owner for personal use: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods given as charity: Dr Charity / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods distributed as free samples: Dr Advertisement / Cr Purchases (at cost).

Goods lost by fire or theft: Dr Loss by Fire (or Loss by Theft) / Cr Purchases. If insured and a claim is admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (amount admitted), Dr Loss by Fire (balance) / Cr Purchases (cost).
Purchases is credited because these goods were bought for sale but will never be sold; the purchases figure is reduced.

example.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 were destroyed by fire. The insurance company admitted a claim of ₹35,000. Journalise.
steps: Total cost of goods lost = ₹50,000: credit Purchases.
Claim admitted ₹35,000: debit Insurance Claim (an asset, receivable).
Loss not covered = 50,000 − 35,000 = ₹15,000: debit Loss by Fire.
example.answer: Dr Insurance Claim ₹35,000, Dr Loss by Fire ₹15,000 / Cr Purchases ₹50,000

learn.reallife: During monsoon floods in Assam, many shops lose stock. Those insured record an insurance claim; the rest record the full loss by flood.

topics.title: Journal entries with GST and set-off of input tax credit

learn.hook: A Delhi gadget dealer pays GST on every purchase and collects GST on every sale. At month-end, she pays the government only the difference. Here is how that shows in the journal.
points: Purchase within the state: Dr Purchases, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Supplier (or Cash). Inter-state purchase: Dr Purchases, Dr Input IGST / Cr Supplier.
Sale within the state: Dr Customer (or Cash) / Cr Sales, Cr Output CGST, Cr Output SGST. Inter-state sale: Cr Output IGST.
GST paid on expenses (e.g. rent, telephone) is also input tax: Dr Expense, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Bank.

Set-off: input IGST is used first against output IGST, then against CGST and SGST. Input CGST is used against output CGST, then IGST. Input SGST is used against output SGST, then IGST. CGST cannot be set off against SGST or vice versa.
Set-off entry: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST (and similarly for SGST). Balance paid: Dr Output CGST, Dr Output SGST / Cr Bank.

example.q: Within Maharashtra, Asha buys goods ₹1,00,000 and sells them for ₹1,50,000; GST 18%. Find CGST payable after set-off and give the set-off entry.
steps: Set-off: Dr Output CGST ₹9,000 / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000 (same for SGST).
example.answer: CGST payable ₹4,500 (and SGST ₹4,500); set-off: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000.

topics.title: The ledger: format, utility and classification of accounts

learn.hook: The journal tells you what happened on 12 June. The ledger tells you how much the business owes Gupta Traders today. Different questions, different books.
points: The ledger is the principal book of accounts. It contains all accounts (cash, debtors, sales, rent and so on), each on a separate page or folio.
Format of a ledger account: debit side (left): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount; credit side (right): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount.
Utility: it shows the net position of each account, such as total sales, total expenses, amount owed by each debtor and to each creditor, and its balances are used to prepare the trial balance.

Journal vs ledger: the journal is the book of original entry, records chronologically, and is the basis of posting; the ledger is the principal book, records analytically by accounts, and is the basis of the trial balance.
Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) are balanced and carried forward; temporary accounts (revenues, expenses) are closed by transfer to the trading and profit and loss account.

example.q: Classify as permanent or temporary: Machinery, Wages, Creditors, Commission received, Capital.
steps: Permanent accounts appear in the balance sheet and continue to the next year: Machinery, Creditors, Capital.
Temporary accounts are closed at year-end to the P&L or trading account: Wages, Commission received.
example.answer: Permanent: Machinery, Creditors, Capital; temporary: Wages, Commission received.

topics.title: Posting from the journal and balancing ledger accounts

learn.hook: Posting is like delivering letters: each journal entry has two addresses, the account debited and the account credited, and each must receive its copy.
points: Posting is transferring journal entries to ledger accounts. In the account debited, write the entry on the debit side as 'To [name of the account credited]'. In the account credited, write it on the credit side as 'By [name of the account debited]'.
Compound entries: each debit and each credit is posted separately. In each account, the other side's accounts are named (for one-to-many entries, each counter account is named with its own amount).
Cross references: L.F. in the journal shows the ledger page; J.F. in the ledger shows the journal page. They prove the posting is done and allow tracing.
Balancing: total both sides, put the difference on the smaller side as 'By/To Balance c/d', and bring it down on the opposite side as 'To/By Balance b/d'.

example.q: Entry: Dr Furniture ₹30,000 / Cr Cash ₹30,000. How is it posted?
steps: Write the ledger page in the journal's L.F. column and the journal page in each account's J.F. column.
example.answer: Furniture A/c Dr side: To Cash ₹30,000; Cash A/c Cr side: By Furniture ₹30,000.

topics.title: The cash book and the simple (single column) cash book

learn.hook: A busy dhaba in Murthal handles hundreds of cash bills a day. Writing a journal entry for each would take forever. The cash book does the job in one line each.
points: The cash book records all cash receipts and cash payments. It is a book of original entry and, at the same time, it is the cash account of the ledger, so no separate cash account is kept.
Simple (single column) cash book: debit side (left) for receipts, credit side (right) for payments. Columns on each side: Date, Particulars, L.F. (or R.No./V.No.), Amount.
Receipts are entered as 'To [account from which cash came]'; payments as 'By [account for which cash was paid]'.
It begins with the opening cash balance on the debit side ('To Balance b/d').
Credit transactions are never entered in the cash book; only cash ones are.

example.q: Cash in hand 1 April ₹20,000. Received from Ravi ₹15,000; paid wages ₹6,000; cash sales ₹9,000; paid rent ₹8,000. Find the closing cash balance.
steps: Balance = 44,000 − 14,000 = ₹30,000, written as 'By Balance c/d' on the credit side.
example.answer: ₹30,000 (debit balance)

topics.title: Double column cash book, cheques and contra entries

learn.hook: Most Indian businesses today hold money in two places: the cash drawer and the bank. A double column cash book tracks both side by side.
points: The double column cash book has two amount columns on each side: Cash and Bank. It replaces both the cash account and the bank account in the ledger.
Cheques received (and deposited the same day) go in the bank column of the debit side; cheques issued go in the bank column of the credit side.

Contra entry: a transaction between cash and bank, recorded on both sides of the cash book and marked 'C' in the L.F. column. Cash deposited into bank: debit bank column 'To Cash', credit cash column 'By Bank'.
Cash withdrawn from bank for office use: debit cash column 'To Bank', credit bank column 'By Cash'.
Contra entries are not posted to the ledger, because both aspects are already in the cash book.

example.q: Cash of ₹25,000 is deposited into the bank. How is it recorded in a double column cash book?
steps: Bank balance rises: debit side, bank column, 'To Cash ₹25,000', L.F. 'C'.
Cash balance falls: credit side, cash column, 'By Bank ₹25,000', L.F. 'C'.
No posting to the ledger is needed.
example.answer: Dr side bank column 'To Cash ₹25,000' (C) and Cr side cash column 'By Bank ₹25,000' (C).

topics.title: Balancing and posting the cash book; bank overdraft

learn.hook: You can never have negative cash in your wallet, but you can owe money to your bank. That single fact explains the trickiest rule of the cash book.
points: Balancing: each column (cash and bank) is totalled separately; the difference is written as 'By Balance c/d' on the smaller side and brought down as 'To Balance b/d'.
The cash column can never show a credit balance, because payments cannot exceed cash available.
The bank column may show a credit balance: that means a bank overdraft, an amount owed to the bank (written as 'To Balance c/d' on the debit side and brought down on the credit side).
Posting: accounts on the debit side of the cash book are credited in the ledger ('By Cash' or 'By Bank'); accounts on the credit side are debited in the ledger ('To Cash' or 'To Bank').
Discount columns (where kept) are memorandum columns: their totals are posted to Discount Allowed (debit) and Discount Received (credit) accounts.

example.q: Bank column totals: debit side ₹60,000, credit side ₹75,000. What is the balance and what does it mean?
steps: The bank has paid ₹15,000 more than the deposits: an overdraft.
Write 'To Balance c/d ₹15,000' on the debit side, bring down 'By Balance b/d ₹15,000' on the credit side.
example.answer: Overdraft (credit balance) of ₹15,000.

topics.title: Petty cash book and the imprest system

learn.hook: The head cashier of a big company shouldn't spend her day paying ₹40 for courier and ₹60 for tea. That job goes to the petty cashier.
points: Petty cash book records small, recurring payments such as postage, stationery, conveyance, cartage and refreshments, kept by a petty cashier.
Advantages: saves the main cashier's time, keeps small payments under control, and allows totals to be posted instead of each item.

Imprest system: the petty cashier is given a fixed amount (imprest) at the start of a period. At the end, the main cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent, so the petty cashier again starts with the full imprest.
Imprest advantages: easy checking, fixed responsibility, limits misuse, and regular reimbursement keeps records up to date.
Analytical petty cash book: separate columns for each expense head. At the end, column totals are posted to the debit of the related expense accounts.

example.q: Imprest ₹5,000. During the week: postage ₹600, stationery ₹1,100, conveyance ₹900, tea ₹450. How much is reimbursed, and what is the balance after reimbursement?
example.answer: Reimbursement ₹3,050; balance after reimbursement ₹5,000.

learn.reallife: At a busy AIIMS department office, a petty cash float covers courier fees and photocopies, topped up every month under the imprest system.

topics.title: Purchases book and purchases return book (with GST)

learn.hook: A Ludhiana bicycle maker buys parts from 50 suppliers on credit every month. One page in the purchases book replaces 50 journal entries.
points: Purchases book (purchases journal) records only credit purchases of goods. Cash purchases go to the cash book; credit purchase of assets goes to the journal proper.

Columns: Date, Invoice No., Name of supplier (Particulars), L.F., Details, Amount. Trade discount is deducted in the details column; only the net amount is recorded. With GST, input CGST and SGST (or IGST) columns or lines are added.
Posting: each supplier's account is credited with the invoice total; the periodic total is debited to Purchases A/c, and GST totals to Input CGST/SGST (or IGST) accounts.
Purchases return book (return outwards book) records goods returned to suppliers out of credit purchases; the source document is the debit note.
Posting the return book: each supplier is debited; the total is credited to Purchases Return A/c, and the GST on returns is credited to the input tax accounts (reversing the credit).

example.q: Bought on credit from Kapoor Traders 50 chairs at ₹1,000 each, trade discount 10%, CGST 9% and SGST 9%. What is entered in the purchases book?
example.answer: Net purchases ₹45,000 + CGST ₹4,050 + SGST ₹4,050 = ₹53,100

learn.reallife: Large retailers such as DMart record thousands of supplier invoices in their purchase registers each week, with GST columns that later feed their GST returns.

topics.title: Sales book and sales return book (with GST)

learn.hook: A Jaipur block-print exporter sells on credit to boutiques all over India. Each invoice is one line in the sales book, and each return is one line in the sales return book.
points: Sales book (sales journal) records only credit sales of goods. The source document is the sales invoice (outward invoice).
Trade discount is deducted in the book; output CGST and SGST (intra-state) or IGST (inter-state) are added.
Posting: each customer's account is debited with the invoice total; the sales total is credited to Sales A/c and the GST totals are credited to Output CGST/SGST/IGST accounts.
Sales return book (return inwards book) records goods returned by customers out of credit sales. The source document is the credit note issued to the customer.
Posting: each customer is credited; the total is debited to Sales Return A/c, and the related output GST accounts are debited.

example.q: Sold on credit to Meera Boutique (Delhi) from Jaipur: 40 kurtis at ₹800 each, trade discount 5%, IGST 5%. What amount is debited to Meera Boutique?
steps: Rajasthan to Delhi is inter-state: IGST 5% = ₹1,520.

topics.title: Journal proper and advantages of special purpose books

learn.hook: Special books handle the daily rush, but some transactions are rare or unusual. They go to the 'leftover' book, the journal proper.
points: Journal proper records transactions that do not fit any special book: opening entries, closing entries, adjustment entries, rectification entries and transfer entries.
It also records credit purchase or sale of assets, bad debts written off, goods withdrawn by the owner, goods lost by fire or theft, and other rare transactions.
Special purpose books: cash book, purchases book, purchases return book, sales book and sales return book.
Advantages of sub-dividing the journal: division of work, specialisation and efficiency, saving of time (totals are posted), easy reference, easier checking and better internal control.

example.q: Which book records each? (a) Bad debts written off ₹2,000, (b) Credit purchase of machinery, (c) Cash sales.
steps: (a) Bad debts are an adjustment, no special book fits: journal proper.
(b) Credit purchase of an asset, not goods: journal proper.
example.answer: (a) Journal proper, (b) journal proper, (c) cash book.

learn.reallife: A cement company's accounts team might have one clerk for the sales register, another for purchases and a third for the cash book, with the senior accountant handling the journal proper.

topics.title: Balancing accounts and reading their balances

learn.hook: A ledger account is like a cricket scoreboard with runs and wickets on two sides. Balancing tells you the score at the end of the innings.
points: Balancing: total both sides, find the difference, write it on the shorter side as 'Balance c/d' so both totals agree, then bring it down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' at the start of the next period.
Debit balance: debit side is larger. Assets, expenses, losses and drawings normally show debit balances.
Credit balance: credit side is larger. Liabilities, capital, incomes and gains normally show credit balances.
A debtor's account normally has a debit balance (he owes us); a creditor's account normally has a credit balance (we owe him).
Nominal (revenue and expense) accounts are not carried forward; they are closed by transfer to the trading or profit and loss account.

example.q: Kamal's account (a customer): Dr: Sales ₹40,000, Sales ₹25,000. Cr: Cash ₹30,000, Sales Return ₹5,000. Balance it.
steps: Balance = ₹30,000 debit: write 'By Balance c/d ₹30,000' on the credit side; bring down 'To Balance b/d ₹30,000'.
example.answer: Debit balance of ₹30,000 (Kamal owes the firm).

learn.reallife: Your mobile wallet shows a running balance after every top-up and payment; an accountant does the same for each ledger account at the period end.

topics.title: Cash book vs pass book and the need for a BRS

learn.hook: Your cash book says you have ₹50,000 in the bank. The bank statement says ₹62,000. Nobody is lying. A bank reconciliation statement finds out why.
points: The business keeps the bank column of its cash book; the bank keeps the business's account in its books and sends a copy, the pass book or bank statement.

The two are mirror images: a deposit is debited in the cash book (bank is our asset) but credited in the pass book (the bank owes us). A withdrawal is credited in the cash book and debited in the pass book.

Favourable balance: debit balance in the cash book = credit balance in the pass book (money in the bank). Unfavourable balance (overdraft): credit balance in the cash book = debit balance in the pass book.
A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) is a statement that explains the differences between the two balances on a date and reconciles them.
Importance: it reveals errors in either record, detects frauds and unauthorised payments, highlights delays in clearing cheques, and confirms the correct bank balance.

example.q: Cash book (bank column) shows a debit balance of ₹40,000. What should the pass book show if both records are complete and correct on the same date?
steps: A debit in the cash book means money held in the bank.
For the bank, that money is a liability to the customer, so it shows a credit.
example.answer: A credit balance of ₹40,000 in the pass book.

learn.reallife: A small exporter in Tiruppur reconciles her bank account with the bank's monthly e-statement to catch delays in export receipts and any wrong charges.

topics.title: Timing differences: cheques not presented and not credited

learn.hook: You hand a cheque to your supplier on 30 March. He deposits it on 3 April. For four days your cash book and bank statement disagree, and that's perfectly normal.
points: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment: the cash book has already reduced the balance; the bank has not. So pass book balance is higher than the cash book balance.
Cheques deposited but not yet collected (credited) by the bank: the cash book has already increased the balance; the bank has not. So pass book balance is lower.
These are timing differences; they disappear when the bank processes the cheques.
Steps in a BRS: start with one balance, add items that make the other balance higher, subtract items that make it lower, and arrive at the other balance.
Starting with the cash book (debit) balance: add cheques issued but not presented; subtract cheques deposited but not credited.

example.q: Cash book balance ₹50,000 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹12,000. Cheques deposited not credited ₹8,000. Find the pass book balance.
steps: Add cheques issued not presented: + ₹12,000 (bank has not paid them yet).
Less cheques deposited not credited: − ₹8,000 (bank has not added them yet).
example.answer: ₹54,000 credit balance as per pass book.

learn.reallife: Cheque Truncation System (CTS) has cut clearing times in India to about a day, but cheques issued on 31 March can still cross into the new financial year.

topics.title: Bank-side items: direct deposits, interest, charges and dishonour

learn.hook: Your bank quietly credits interest, debits SMS charges and pays your insurance premium by standing instruction. You find out only when the statement arrives.
points: Direct deposits by customers into the firm's bank account (e.g. NEFT/UPI receipts): recorded by the bank first, so pass book balance is higher.
Interest allowed and dividends collected by the bank on the firm's behalf: pass book higher.
Bank charges, interest on overdraft, and direct payments made by the bank under standing instructions (insurance premium, EMI): pass book lower.
Cheque deposited and dishonoured: the cash book shows it as deposited, but the bank reverses (debits) it, so pass book is lower.
Starting from the cash book (Dr): add direct deposits, interest and dividends credited; subtract bank charges, direct payments, interest on overdraft and dishonoured cheques.

example.q: Cash book ₹60,000 (Dr). Bank charged ₹500; interest credited ₹1,200; a customer paid ₹7,000 directly; insurance premium ₹3,000 paid by bank. Pass book balance?

learn.reallife: Many Indian households set standing instructions for SIPs and loan EMIs; the debit hits the bank account before anyone writes it in a cash book.

topics.title: Preparing a BRS from the cash book or the pass book balance

learn.hook: Two roads lead to the same destination. You can start a BRS from the cash book or from the pass book; with the right signs, you land on the other balance exactly.
points: Format: Bank Reconciliation Statement as on [date]. Particulars | Plus items (₹) | Minus items (₹). Start with the given balance, list additions and subtractions, and end with the balance as per the other record.

From cash book Dr balance: add cheques issued not presented, direct deposits, interest and dividends credited by bank. Subtract cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques.

From pass book Cr balance: reverse every sign. Add cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques; subtract cheques issued not presented, direct deposits, interest credited.
Quick test: for each item ask, 'Which record has it already? Does it make that record's balance bigger or smaller?'

example.q: Pass book ₹90,000 (Cr). Cheques deposited not credited ₹15,000; cheques issued not presented ₹22,000; bank charges ₹600; interest credited ₹1,600. Find the cash book balance.
steps: Add: deposits not credited 15,000 + bank charges 600 = 15,600.

learn.reallife: Treasury teams at companies like Tata Steel reconcile dozens of bank accounts every month with software that applies these same plus-and-minus rules.

topics.title: Overdraft BRS and errors in the cash book or pass book

learn.hook: An overdraft is a minus balance. Treat it like a negative number on a number line, apply the usual adjustments, and the BRS works just the same.
points: Overdraft as per cash book = credit balance in the cash book; overdraft as per pass book = debit balance in the pass book.

Starting with overdraft as per cash book: add cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, interest on overdraft, direct payments and dishonoured cheques (they increase the overdraft); subtract cheques issued not presented, direct deposits and interest credited (they reduce it). The result is the overdraft as per pass book.
Shortcut: treat an overdraft as a negative balance and use the normal favourable-balance signs; a negative result is an overdraft.

Errors by the business: e.g. a deposit of ₹5,400 entered as ₹4,500 makes the cash book ₹900 lower, so starting from the cash book add ₹900. Overcasting the receipts side overstates the cash book, so subtract.
Errors by the bank: e.g. the bank wrongly debits another customer's cheque to our account, making the pass book lower; starting from the cash book, subtract it.

example.q: Overdraft as per cash book ₹30,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹8,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹5,000; interest on overdraft ₹1,000 charged by bank. Overdraft as per pass book?
steps: Cheques issued not presented reduce the overdraft in the bank's books: −30,000 + 8,000 = −22,000.
Cheques not credited and interest increase the overdraft: −22,000 − 5,000 − 1,000 = −28,000.
example.answer: Overdraft of ₹28,000 as per pass book.

learn.reallife: Small businesses with a cash-credit limit from a cooperative bank often run on overdraft; their BRS starts from a credit balance in the cash book.

topics.title: Amended cash book and BRS from the amended balance

learn.hook: Some differences are the cash book's own fault: unrecorded bank charges, direct deposits, dishonoured cheques. Fix those in the cash book first, then reconcile only what's left.
points: Amended (adjusted) cash book: before preparing the BRS, the cash book is corrected for items the bank has recorded but the firm has not, and for the firm's own errors.

Debit side additions: direct deposits, interest and dividends collected by bank, errors that understated the balance. Credit side additions: bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques, interest on overdraft, errors that overstated the balance.
Items NOT corrected in the cash book: cheques issued not presented, cheques deposited not credited, and errors made by the bank. These remain in the BRS.
BRS from the amended balance contains only these remaining items and ends with the pass book balance.
Advantage: the corrected cash book balance is the true bank balance shown in the balance sheet.

example.q: Cash book ₹40,000 (Dr). Bank charges ₹500; interest credited ₹1,500; cheque dishonoured ₹3,000; unpresented cheques ₹6,000. Find the amended balance and the pass book balance.
steps: BRS from amended balance: add unpresented cheques 6,000.
example.answer: Amended balance ₹38,000; pass book ₹44,000.

learn.reallife: Auditors of Indian companies ask for the adjusted bank balance, not the raw cash book figure, before signing off the balance sheet.

chapters.title: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors

topics.title: Trial balance: meaning, format and objectives

learn.hook: After a month of entries, how do you know your books are at least arithmetically right? You line up every ledger balance and check that debits equal credits.
points: A trial balance is a statement of the debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts on a particular date. Under double entry, total debits must equal total credits.
Format: S. No. | Account title | L.F. | Debit balance (₹) | Credit balance (₹). Heading: 'Trial Balance of [firm] as on [date]'.

Objectives: (1) ascertain the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts; (2) help in locating errors; (3) give a summary of all ledger accounts in one place; (4) help in preparing financial statements.
It is a statement, not an account, and it can be prepared on any date, not only at the year-end.

example.q: Ledger balances on 31 March: Cash ₹20,000 (Dr), Capital ₹1,00,000 (Cr), Purchases ₹90,000 (Dr), Sales ₹1,30,000 (Cr), Furniture ₹40,000 (Dr), Creditors ₹30,000 (Cr), Rent ₹10,000 (Dr), Debtors ₹1,00,000 (Dr). Does the trial balance agree?
steps: Both totals are ₹2,60,000: the trial balance agrees.
example.answer: Yes, both sides total ₹2,60,000.

learn.reallife: Before closing its quarterly results, a listed company like Hindustan Unilever runs a trial balance from its ERP system; a mismatch means someone checks the postings before results go out.

topics.title: Preparing a trial balance by the balances method

learn.hook: There's a simple memory hook for trial balances: DEAL CRIL. Drawings, Expenses, Assets, Losses on the debit side; Capital, Revenues, Incomes, Liabilities on the credit side.
points: Balances method (the method used in the CBSE syllabus): list each ledger account's closing balance in the debit or credit column.
Debit balances: assets, expenses, losses, drawings, purchases, sales returns, opening stock, debtors, discount allowed.
Credit balances: capital, liabilities, incomes, gains, sales, purchases returns, creditors, bank overdraft, discount received, provisions.

Opening stock appears in the trial balance (it is a ledger balance). Closing stock normally appears outside the trial balance as an adjustment; it appears inside only if purchases are already adjusted for it.
Correcting a wrong trial balance: move each balance to its proper side, then re-total.

example.q: Prepare totals: Opening stock ₹25,000; Purchases ₹1,20,000; Sales ₹1,80,000; Returns inwards ₹5,000; Returns outwards ₹3,000; Capital ₹1,00,000; Furniture ₹43,000; Debtors ₹60,000; Creditors ₹30,000; Salary ₹40,000; Discount received ₹2,000; Cash ₹22,000.
example.answer: Both sides ₹3,15,000.
