topics.title: Agreement of the trial balance and searching for errors

learn.hook: A trial balance that agrees is like a cricket scoreboard that adds up: it doesn't prove the umpire got every decision right.
points: Agreement of totals proves only arithmetical accuracy, not that the books are correct.

Errors NOT disclosed: complete omission of a transaction, errors of principle, compensating errors, recording a wrong amount in the book of original entry, posting to the wrong account but on the correct side.

Errors disclosed (one-sided): wrong totalling of a subsidiary book or account, posting a wrong amount to one account, posting to the wrong side, omitting to post one side, wrong balancing, omitting a balance from the trial balance.
Searching: re-total the trial balance; check that every balance is included and on the correct side; re-check totals of subsidiary books and balances of accounts; check postings.
Tips: halve the difference and look for an item of that amount posted to the wrong side; if the difference is divisible by 9, look for transposed digits (e.g. 54 written as 45) or a slide error.

example.q: A trial balance shows a difference of ₹1,800. A cheque for ₹900 received from a customer may have been posted to the debit of his account. Is that consistent?
steps: Posting ₹900 to the wrong side shifts the total by twice the amount.
So it is a likely cause: check the customer's account.
example.answer: Yes: a wrong-side posting creates a difference of double the amount, 2 × ₹900 = ₹1,800.

learn.reallife: Auditors at the Comptroller and Auditor General's office still use the 'divide by 9' trick when checking manually kept government ledgers.

quiz.mistake: Thinks any wrong amount causes a difference

topics.title: Types of errors: commission, omission, principle, compensating

learn.hook: Errors come in families. Knowing which family an error belongs to tells you at once whether the trial balance will catch it and how to fix it.
points: Errors of commission: wrong recording, posting, totalling, balancing or carrying forward, e.g. wrong amount, wrong account (of the same class) or wrong side.
Errors of omission: complete omission (transaction not recorded at all; trial balance not affected) or partial omission (one side not posted; trial balance affected).
Errors of principle: violating accounting principles, mainly confusing capital and revenue items, e.g. purchase of furniture debited to Purchases, or repairs debited to Machinery.
Compensating errors: two or more errors that cancel each other's effect, e.g. Rahul's account debited ₹100 short and Sunil's account debited ₹100 in excess.
Classification for rectification: one-sided errors affect one account only (and usually the trial balance); two-sided errors affect two or more accounts (and usually not the trial balance).

example.q: Classify: (a) ₹10,000 paid for a computer debited to Office Expenses; (b) credit sale of ₹2,000 to Leena not recorded at all; (c) sales book totalled ₹100 short.
steps: (a) Capital expenditure treated as revenue: error of principle.
(b) Transaction never recorded: complete error of omission.
example.answer: (a) Principle, (b) omission (complete), (c) commission.

learn.reallife: Large firms run monthly checks on whether new laptops were wrongly booked as 'office expenses', a classic error of principle that understates assets and profit.

topics.title: Rectification before the trial balance: one-sided and two-sided errors

learn.hook: Fixing errors is like fixing a recipe: if one ingredient was wrong, you adjust only that; if two were swapped, you fix both together.
points: One-sided errors found before the trial balance is prepared: rectified by an explanatory entry (a note) on the appropriate side of the affected account, without a journal entry. E.g. sales book undercast ₹500: write 'By Undercasting of sales book ₹500' on the credit side of Sales account.

Two-sided errors: rectified by a journal entry. Method: (1) write the wrong entry made; (2) write the correct entry that should have been made; (3) rectifying entry = debit the account short-debited or over-credited, credit the account over-debited or short-credited.
Example: credit sale to Ram ₹2,000 posted to Shyam's account: Dr Ram / Cr Shyam ₹2,000.
Error of principle: repairs ₹5,000 debited to Building: Dr Repairs / Cr Building ₹5,000.
Complete omission: simply record the correct entry now.

example.q: Furniture bought for ₹12,000 was debited to Purchases. Give the rectifying entry.
steps: Wrong entry: Dr Purchases / Cr Cash ₹12,000.
Correct entry: Dr Furniture / Cr Cash ₹12,000.
Cash is correct; Purchases is wrongly debited, and Furniture is not debited.
example.answer: Dr Furniture ₹12,000 / Cr Purchases ₹12,000

learn.reallife: Software at banks like Canara Bank never deletes a wrong entry; it posts a correcting entry, keeping a full audit trail, exactly the approach of rectification.

topics.title: Suspense account: opening it and rectifying through it

learn.hook: When the trial balance won't agree and the deadline is tomorrow, accountants park the difference in a temporary waiting room called the suspense account.
points: If the trial balance does not agree and errors cannot be found at once, the difference is placed in a suspense account to make the totals agree temporarily.
If the debit side is short, the suspense account shows a debit balance; if the credit side is short, it shows a credit balance.

After the trial balance, one-sided errors are rectified through the suspense account. E.g. purchases book overcast ₹700: Dr Suspense / Cr Purchases ₹700. Discount allowed ₹200 not posted to Discount account: Dr Discount Allowed / Cr Suspense ₹200.
Two-sided errors are rectified without the suspense account.
Once all errors are corrected, the suspense account closes. The original difference can be found from the balancing figure of the suspense account.

example.q: Trial balance: debit ₹1,48,500, credit ₹1,50,000. Later found: (i) purchases book undercast ₹1,000; (ii) payment of ₹250 to Ravi not posted to his account; (iii) discount allowed ₹250 not posted to Discount Allowed account. Show that the suspense account closes.
steps: Difference = ₹1,500, debit side short: Suspense shows a debit balance of ₹1,500.
example.answer: The suspense account closes: debit ₹1,500 = credits ₹1,500.

learn.reallife: At the year-end close, many Indian SMEs see a small suspense balance in their trial balance; their CA's job is to trace and clear it before filing returns.

topics.title: Rectification after final accounts and the effect on profit

learn.hook: An error found after the books are closed can't be fixed in last year's P&L account. Instead, it goes into a special account that adjusts the profit next year.
points: Errors in nominal (revenue and expense) accounts change profit. Errors only between real or personal accounts do not change profit.
If an expense is overstated or an income understated, profit is understated; rectification increases profit (and vice versa).

Examples: furniture ₹10,000 debited to Purchases understates profit by ₹10,000; rectification raises profit by ₹10,000. Sales book undercast ₹2,000 understates profit; rectification raises it by ₹2,000.

After final accounts are prepared, nominal accounts are already closed, so rectification of such errors is made through a Profit and Loss Adjustment account; its balance is transferred to the capital account.
Corrected profit = Profit as shown + increases from rectifications − decreases from rectifications.

example.q: Profit shown ₹1,00,000. Errors: (a) purchase of machinery ₹20,000 debited to Purchases; (b) sales returns ₹3,000 not recorded (two-sided omission); (c) rent ₹5,000 debited to the landlord's personal account. Find the corrected profit.

learn.reallife: When a listed company finds a past error, accounting standards require it to restate figures or disclose the correction, because investors rely on profit numbers.

chapters.title: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves

topics.title: Meaning and features of depreciation

learn.hook: A brand-new delivery van bought for ₹8 lakh will not be worth ₹8 lakh after five years of Mumbai traffic. Accounting must recognise that steady decline. That is depreciation.
points: Depreciation is the decline in the value of a fixed (depreciable) asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is the allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life.

Features: it reduces the book value of the asset; it is a non-cash expense (no cash goes out when it is charged); it is a continuing process over the asset's life; it applies to fixed assets only, not to current assets like stock.
Depreciation is charged to the profit and loss account as an expense of each year of use.
Land is not depreciated, because it normally has an unlimited useful life and does not get used up. Buildings on the land are depreciated.

example.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹5,00,000 with a 10-year life and no scrap value. How much depreciation is charged per year, and is cash paid each year?
steps: This amount is charged to the P&L account every year.
No cash goes out when depreciation is charged; the cash was paid when the machine was bought.
example.answer: ₹50,000 a year; it is a non-cash expense.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways depreciates its coaches and locomotives over decades of service, but not the land under its stations.

topics.title: Depletion, amortisation and causes of depreciation

learn.hook: Coal India mines coal, a pharma company holds a 20-year patent, and a call centre buys computers. All three lose asset value, but accountants use three different words for it.
points: Depletion: reduction in the value of wasting (natural) assets such as mines, quarries and oil wells, as the resources are extracted. It is usually based on the quantity extracted.
Amortisation: writing off the cost of intangible assets such as patents, copyrights, trademarks and goodwill over their useful life.

Causes of depreciation: (1) wear and tear due to use or passage of time; (2) expiration of legal rights (leases, patents, copyrights); (3) obsolescence, when an asset becomes outdated because of new technology or changes in demand; (4) abnormal factors such as accidents, fire, flood or earthquake.
Depletion is calculated by: (Cost ÷ Total estimated quantity) × Quantity extracted in the year.

example.q: A mine costing ₹50,00,000 is estimated to contain 1,00,000 tonnes of ore. 8,000 tonnes are extracted this year. Find depletion.

learn.reallife: When smartphones replaced feature phones, many Indian factories making keypad phones saw their machines become obsolete long before they physically wore out.

topics.title: Need for depreciation and factors in measuring it

learn.hook: If a taxi owner ignored the wearing out of his cab, he'd think he was richer every year, until the day the cab died and he had no money for a new one.
points: Need: (1) matching the cost of the asset with the revenue it helps earn, for correct profit; (2) tax: depreciation is an allowable deduction for income tax; (3) true and fair financial position: assets are not overstated; (4) compliance with law (the Companies Act requires it); (5) retaining funds for replacement, since profit available for distribution is reduced.
Cost of asset (depreciable cost base): purchase price plus all costs to bring it to working condition: freight, cartage, installation, commission, registration.
Estimated net residual (scrap) value: expected sale value at the end of its life, less disposal costs.
Estimated useful life: the period (or production units) over which the asset is expected to be used.
Depreciable amount = Cost − Net residual value.

example.q: A machine is bought for ₹4,50,000; freight ₹15,000; installation ₹35,000. Estimated scrap ₹50,000; life 9 years. Find the depreciable amount and annual depreciation (equal instalments).
example.answer: Depreciable amount ₹4,50,000; ₹50,000 a year.

learn.reallife: An app-cab fleet owner in Hyderabad sets aside the depreciation amount every year so that when the cars wear out, the business can afford new ones.

topics.title: Straight line method (SLM)

learn.hook: Under the straight line method, depreciation is the same every year, like a fixed monthly SIP. Plot the book value on a graph and you get a straight line sloping down.
points: Straight line (fixed instalment or original cost) method: equal depreciation every year. Annual depreciation = (Cost − Net residual value) ÷ Estimated useful life.
Rate of depreciation under SLM = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100. Depreciation can also be found as Cost × Rate ÷ 100.
Advantages: simple to calculate; the asset can be written down to zero (or scrap value) at the end of its life; suitable where use is even across years.

Limitations: ignores the fact that repairs rise as assets age, so the total charge (depreciation + repairs) rises in later years; does not consider the effective use of the asset; interest on capital invested is ignored.
Suitable for: patents, copyrights, leases and furniture, i.e. assets whose usefulness falls evenly with time.

example.q: Cost ₹1,60,000; scrap ₹10,000; life 5 years. Find annual depreciation, the rate, and book value after 2 years.

learn.reallife: A coaching institute in Kota writes off its classroom furniture and its 10-year lease equally each year: the straight line method suits both.

topics.title: Written down value method (WDV) and comparison with SLM

learn.hook: Under WDV, depreciation is big in the early years and shrinks later, much like a new phone that loses the most value in its first year.
points: Written down value (reducing or diminishing balance) method: a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value each year. Depreciation falls every year.
Under WDV the book value never reaches zero.

Advantages: total charge (depreciation + repairs) stays fairly even, since high depreciation in early years meets low repairs, and vice versa; accepted by income tax authorities; suitable where obsolescence is fast.
Limitations: the asset cannot be fully written off; finding a suitable rate is difficult; calculations are more involved.

Comparison: SLM charges on original cost, equal amounts, book value can become zero, suits patents, leases, furniture. WDV charges on reducing book value, decreasing amounts, never zero, suits plant, machinery, vehicles, and is recognised by income tax law.

example.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; WDV rate 20%. Find depreciation for 3 years and the book value at the end of year 3.

learn.reallife: Income tax rules in India prescribe WDV rates for blocks of assets; for example, vehicles and computers are grouped into blocks with their own rates.

topics.title: Depreciation for part of a year, additions and repairs

learn.hook: Buy a machine on 1 October and close books on 31 March, and it has worked for you for exactly six months. Depreciation must count those months, not the full year.
points: When an asset is bought during the year, depreciation is charged from the date of purchase to the end of the year: Depreciation = Cost × Rate × Months used ÷ 12 (under SLM; under WDV, on the book value).
Count months carefully: bought 1 July, year ending 31 March: July to March = 9 months. Bought 1 January: 3 months.
If a question says the rate is 'per annum', time is always prorated; if it says depreciation is charged for a full year regardless, follow the instruction.
Additions or extensions that increase capacity or life (a new wing, an extra unit) are capitalised and depreciated separately from their date of addition.
Ordinary repairs and maintenance that only keep an asset working are revenue expenses, charged to P&L; they are not added to the asset.

example.q: On 1 April 2025 a firm has machinery ₹4,00,000. On 1 October 2025 it adds a machine for ₹1,20,000. Depreciation 10% p.a. SLM; year ends 31 March 2026. Find depreciation for 2025-26.

topics.title: Recording depreciation: asset account vs provision for depreciation

learn.hook: Two firms buy the same ₹1,00,000 machine. After 3 years, one balance sheet shows 'Machinery ₹70,000'; the other shows 'Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision ₹30,000'. Same truth, two styles.
points: Method 1: charging depreciation to the asset account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset account shows the reduced book value each year.

Method 2: creating a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Provision for Depreciation; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset stays at original cost.
Balance sheet (method 1): asset at written down value. Balance sheet (method 2): asset at cost, less provision for depreciation (accumulated), showing net book value.
Advantage of method 2: original cost and total depreciation to date are both visible at a glance, which helps for insurance, tax and replacement decisions.

example.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a. Show the balance sheet position on 31 March 2026 under both methods.
steps: Method 2: Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision for depreciation ₹30,000 = ₹70,000.
example.answer: ₹70,000 net under both; method 2 also shows cost ₹1,00,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹30,000.

learn.reallife: Schedule III statements of companies like Bajaj Auto show gross block, accumulated depreciation and net block for each class of asset, which is method 2 in action.

topics.title: Disposal of an asset: book value, profit or loss, disposal account

learn.hook: Selling an old machine is like selling a used bike: whether you 'profit' depends on what it's worth in your books today, not what you paid for it years ago.
points: Steps: find the book value on the date of sale (cost less depreciation up to that date, including depreciation for the part of the year before sale).
Profit on sale = Sale price − Book value (credited to P&L). Loss on sale = Book value − Sale price (debited to P&L).
Entries (asset account method): Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset (for the part year); Dr Bank / Cr Asset (sale proceeds); for profit Dr Asset / Cr P&L; for loss Dr P&L / Cr Asset.

Asset disposal account: transfer the asset's cost (Dr Disposal / Cr Asset), its accumulated depreciation (Dr Provision / Cr Disposal) and sale proceeds (Dr Bank / Cr Disposal); the balance is profit or loss, transferred to P&L.
Partial sale: only the part sold is removed with its depreciation; the remaining assets continue to be depreciated in full.

example.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Sold on 1 October 2025 for ₹70,000. Find profit or loss.
example.answer: Loss of ₹5,000

learn.reallife: When State Transport Corporations auction old buses, each sale is compared with the bus's book value to decide profit or loss on disposal.

topics.title: Disposal with provision for depreciation and insurance claims

learn.hook: When a fire destroys a machine, the insurer pays only part of its value. Accounting must show three things: the depreciation written back, the claim and the loss that's left.
points: When a provision for depreciation account is kept, the accumulated depreciation on the asset sold is transferred: Dr Provision for Depreciation / Cr Asset (or Cr Asset Disposal).
The asset account is then credited with sale proceeds and the balance is profit or loss, or all items are collected in an asset disposal account.

Asset destroyed by fire or accident: find book value on that date. Insurance claim admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (or Insurance Company) / Cr Asset (or Disposal). Uncovered loss: Dr Loss by Fire (to P&L) / Cr Asset.
Loss by fire = Book value on the date of fire − Insurance claim admitted (− any scrap value realised).

example.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; accumulated depreciation ₹80,000. Destroyed by fire; insurer admits ₹90,000. Find the loss and pass the entries (provision method).
steps: Dr Provision for Depreciation ₹80,000 / Cr Machinery ₹80,000.
Loss = 1,20,000 − 90,000 = ₹30,000: Dr Loss by Fire (P&L) / Cr Machinery ₹30,000.
example.answer: Loss of ₹30,000

topics.title: Provisions and the provision for doubtful debts

learn.hook: Some customers who owe you money will never pay. You don't know who yet, but experience says about 5%. A provision lets you face that loss before it hits.
points: A provision is an amount charged against profit to provide for a known liability or a likely loss whose amount cannot be determined with certainty.
Examples: provision for depreciation, provision for bad and doubtful debts, provision for taxation, provision for repairs and renewals, provision for discount on debtors.
Bad debts written off: Dr Bad Debts / Cr Debtor; then Dr P&L / Cr Bad Debts. Creating a provision: Dr P&L / Cr Provision for Doubtful Debts.

When a provision already exists, bad debts are transferred to it: Dr Provision for Doubtful Debts / Cr Bad Debts. The charge to P&L = Bad debts + New provision − Old provision. If negative, the excess is credited to P&L.
New provision is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts. In the balance sheet: Debtors less Provision.

example.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; new provision 5%; old provision ₹6,000; bad debts during the year ₹4,000. Find the P&L charge.
steps: Debtors after further bad debts = ₹1,90,000; new provision = 5% = ₹9,500.
example.answer: ₹17,500 debited to P&L.

learn.reallife: RBI requires banks to make provisions on loans that turn doubtful; that is why bank results in India report 'provisions' as a separate charge against profit.

topics.title: Reserves and how they differ from provisions

learn.hook: A provision is like an umbrella you must buy because rain is forecast. A reserve is like extra savings you choose to keep from your pocket money, just in case.
points: A reserve is an amount set aside out of profit (an appropriation of profit) to strengthen the financial position, meet contingencies or for specific purposes. It is created after profit is ascertained.
Provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Provision is made for a known liability or expected loss; reserve is made to strengthen the business or meet future needs, with no specific liability in mind (except specific reserves).
Provision is shown as a deduction from the related asset or under liabilities; reserve is shown under 'Reserves and Surplus' on the liabilities side.
Provision must be made even if there is a loss; reserve is created only when there is profit. Provisions cannot be used for dividend; some revenue reserves can be.

example.q: Net profit ₹5,00,000 after charging provision for doubtful debts ₹20,000. The owner transfers ₹50,000 to general reserve. Which is a charge and which is an appropriation?
steps: Provision ₹20,000 was deducted to arrive at profit: a charge against profit.
₹50,000 transferred out of profit after it was ascertained: an appropriation of profit.
example.answer: Provision: charge against profit; reserve: appropriation of profit.

learn.reallife: Banks like SBI transfer a part of their profits to statutory reserves each year: an appropriation that strengthens their capital base.

topics.title: Types of reserves and secret reserves

learn.hook: Some reserves come from everyday trading profit, some from rare capital gains, and some are hidden from view altogether. Each has a different job.
points: Revenue reserves are created out of revenue (trading) profits, e.g. general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve. They can be used for any purpose, including dividends.

Capital reserves are created out of capital profits, e.g. premium on issue of shares or debentures, profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on reissue of forfeited shares, profit prior to incorporation, profit on revaluation of assets. They are generally not available for dividends and are used to write off capital losses.

General reserve: not for any specific purpose. Specific reserves: for a stated purpose, e.g. dividend equalisation reserve, debenture redemption reserve, workmen compensation fund, investment fluctuation fund.
Importance of reserves: meet unforeseen losses, strengthen financial position, help expansion, stabilise dividends, redeem long-term liabilities.

Secret reserve: a reserve not shown in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overstating liabilities, e.g. excessive depreciation, undervaluing stock, excessive provision for doubtful debts, charging capital expenditure to revenue. Merits: hides fluctuations and strengthens position. Demerits: hides true profit and position, can be misused, and goes against full disclosure and the requirement of a true and fair view.

example.q: A firm charges depreciation at 25% on a machine when 10% is reasonable. Machine cost ₹4,00,000. What secret reserve is created in year 1 (SLM basis)?
steps: Excess = 1,00,000 − 40,000 = ₹60,000: profit is understated and the asset undervalued by this amount.
example.answer: Secret reserve of ₹60,000

learn.reallife: Banks and insurers in India must disclose their reserves clearly; hidden cushions are discouraged because depositors and policyholders rely on true accounts.

topics.title: Financial statements and their users

learn.hook: All the journalising, posting and balancing of a year leads to two pages: the profit and loss story and the balance sheet snapshot. Those two pages are what everyone wants to read.
points: Financial statements are the end product of the accounting process. For a sole proprietor they are the trading and profit and loss account (performance for a period) and the balance sheet (position on a date).
Objectives: to find the profit or loss of the period, to show the financial position, and to provide information to stakeholders for decisions.

Stakeholders and needs: owners (profit, safety of capital); management (control and planning); lenders (repaying capacity, security); creditors (short-term liquidity); government (tax, policy); employees (job security, bonus); investors (returns, growth).
Importance for a sole proprietor: tells him how much he earned, how much he can draw, what he owns and owes, supports loan applications and tax returns, and helps plan growth.

example.q: A grocer wants a bank loan to open a second shop. What two statements will the bank ask for, and what does each tell it?
steps: Trading and profit and loss account: whether the shop earns enough profit to pay interest and instalments.
Balance sheet: what the grocer owns and owes on a date, i.e. the security behind the loan.
example.answer: The trading and P&L account (earning power) and the balance sheet (financial position).

topics.title: Capital, revenue and deferred revenue expenditure

learn.hook: Paying ₹50 lakh for a new printing machine and paying ₹5,000 to oil it are both 'spending', yet one sits in the balance sheet for years and the other vanishes into this year's P&L.
points: Capital expenditure: spent to acquire or improve fixed assets, or to increase earning capacity; benefit lasts more than one year. Shown as an asset in the balance sheet. Examples: buying machinery, freight and installation on it, building extension, legal charges on buying land.
Revenue expenditure: spent on day-to-day running; benefit is used up within the year. Charged to the trading or P&L account. Examples: wages, salaries, rent, repairs, insurance, carriage on goods.
Deferred revenue expenditure: revenue in nature but so large that its benefit is spread over several years, e.g. a heavy advertising campaign to launch a product. It is written off over those years.
Tests: does it create or improve an asset? Is it recurring? How long does the benefit last? Does it increase earning capacity?

example.q: Classify: (a) wages paid to workers who installed a new machine; (b) wages paid to factory workers for production; (c) ₹30 lakh TV campaign whose effect will last 3 years.
steps: (a) Brings the machine into working condition: capital expenditure.
(c) Revenue in nature but long benefit: deferred revenue expenditure, written off over 3 years.
example.answer: (a) Capital, (b) revenue, (c) deferred revenue.

learn.reallife: When Indian Railways electrifies a route, the cost is capital expenditure; the electricity bill to run the trains afterwards is revenue expenditure.

topics.title: Capital receipts and revenue receipts

learn.hook: A shop gets ₹5 lakh from selling biscuits and ₹5 lakh from selling an old freezer. Same cash, very different meaning.
points: Revenue receipts arise from the normal business operations: sales of goods, commission, rent, interest and dividends received. They are credited to the trading or P&L account.
Capital receipts arise from sources other than normal operations: capital introduced by the owner, loans received, sale proceeds of fixed assets. They affect the balance sheet.
Capital receipts either increase a liability (loan, capital) or reduce an asset (sale of a fixed asset).
Only the profit or loss on sale of a fixed asset (sale price minus book value) goes to the P&L account; the full proceeds are a capital receipt.
Classification matters: treating a capital receipt as revenue overstates profit.

example.q: A firm sells an old car with book value ₹2,00,000 for ₹2,30,000. How much is a capital receipt and how much goes to the P&L?
steps: The full ₹2,30,000 is a capital receipt (sale of a fixed asset).
Profit on sale = 2,30,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹30,000, credited to P&L as a gain.
The car (₹2,00,000) is removed from the balance sheet.
example.answer: Capital receipt ₹2,30,000; ₹30,000 profit to P&L.

learn.reallife: When a startup raises money from venture capital investors, that is a capital receipt; the subscription fees from its customers are revenue receipts.

topics.title: Trading account: gross profit and cost of goods sold

learn.hook: The trading account answers one question: how much did we earn just by buying and selling goods, before office rent and salaries?
points: Trading account shows gross profit or gross loss from trading. Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold.

Debit side: opening stock; purchases less purchases returns; direct expenses: carriage inwards, freight inwards, wages, fuel and power, import duty, octroi, royalty on production, gas and water for the factory.
Credit side: sales less sales returns; closing stock.
Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock.
If the credit side exceeds the debit side, the difference is gross profit (transferred to P&L credit); if not, gross loss (to P&L debit).

example.q: Opening stock ₹40,000; purchases ₹2,00,000; purchases returns ₹10,000; wages ₹30,000; carriage inwards ₹5,000; sales ₹3,50,000; sales returns ₹15,000; closing stock ₹50,000. Find COGS and gross profit.
example.answer: COGS ₹2,15,000; gross profit ₹1,20,000.

learn.reallife: A Firozabad bangle maker's trading account carries fuel for the furnaces and wages of the artisans as direct expenses, because they are part of making the goods.

topics.title: Profit and loss account: net profit or net loss

learn.hook: Gross profit is the cake. The profit and loss account cuts out slices for rent, salaries, advertising and interest. What's left is net profit.
points: The profit and loss account starts with gross profit (credit side) or gross loss (debit side).

Debit side: indirect expenses and losses. Office and administration (salaries, office rent, printing and stationery, telephone, audit fees); selling and distribution (carriage outwards, advertisement, salesmen's commission, bad debts); financial (interest on loan, discount allowed, bank charges); depreciation; losses (loss by fire, loss on sale of assets).
Credit side: other incomes and gains: discount received, commission received, rent received, interest received, dividends, profit on sale of assets.
Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Indirect expenses and losses.
Net profit is transferred to the credit of the capital account (net loss to the debit).

example.q: Gross profit ₹1,20,000; salaries ₹40,000; rent ₹18,000; advertisement ₹7,000; discount received ₹3,000; interest on loan ₹6,000; commission received ₹8,000. Find net profit.

topics.title: Closing entries

learn.hook: At the end of the year, every income and expense account must be emptied into the trading and P&L accounts, like pouring many small jars into two big ones.
points: Closing entries transfer the balances of nominal (revenue and expense) accounts to the trading account and P&L account, so those accounts are closed.

Trading account debits: Dr Trading / Cr Opening Stock, Purchases, Wages, Carriage Inwards, other direct expenses. Sales: Dr Sales / Cr Trading. Returns: Dr Purchases Return / Cr Purchases (or Cr Trading); Dr Sales / Cr Sales Return (or Dr Trading / Cr Sales Return).
Closing stock: Dr Closing Stock / Cr Trading. (Closing stock becomes an asset carried to the balance sheet.)
Gross profit: Dr Trading / Cr P&L. Indirect expenses: Dr P&L / Cr each expense account. Incomes: Dr each income account / Cr P&L.
Net profit: Dr P&L / Cr Capital. Net loss: Dr Capital / Cr P&L. Drawings: Dr Capital / Cr Drawings.

example.q: Give closing entries for: Sales ₹5,00,000; Salaries ₹60,000; Commission received ₹10,000; Net profit ₹80,000.
example.answer: As listed: sales and incomes debited, expenses credited, and net profit credited to capital.

topics.title: Operating profit (EBIT)

learn.hook: Two tea companies earn the same net profit. One earns it from selling tea; the other mostly from selling a plot of land. Operating profit tells you which one is really good at business.
points: Operating profit is the profit earned from the normal operating activities of the business, ignoring non-operating items.
Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses − Non-operating incomes.

Non-operating expenses: interest on loans, loss on sale of fixed assets, loss by fire. Non-operating incomes: interest and dividends on investments, profit on sale of fixed assets, rent received from non-business property.
It is also called earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) when computed before interest and tax: EBIT = Net profit before tax + Interest.
Operating profit helps compare the true operating efficiency of firms.

example.q: Net profit ₹1,50,000; interest on loan ₹20,000; loss on sale of machine ₹10,000; dividend received ₹15,000; profit on sale of land ₹25,000. Find operating profit.

topics.title: Balance sheet: format and classification

learn.hook: The P&L account is a movie of the year. The balance sheet is a photograph taken on the last day: everything owned, everything owed, frozen at that moment.
points: The balance sheet is a statement of financial position on a particular date. In the horizontal form used for sole proprietors, liabilities and capital are on the left and assets on the right.

Assets: non-current assets: fixed assets, tangible (land, building, machinery, furniture, vehicles) and intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks); long-term investments. Current assets: stock, debtors, bills receivable, cash, bank, prepaid expenses, short-term investments.
Liabilities: non-current (long-term loans) and current (creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses).
Capital is shown as: Opening capital + Additional capital + Net profit − Drawings (− Net loss).
Flow: ledger balances → trial balance → trading and P&L account (nominal items) → balance sheet (real and personal items, plus closing stock and the adjusted capital).

example.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000; net profit ₹80,000; drawings ₹30,000. Assets total ₹4,50,000. Find closing capital and total liabilities.
example.answer: Closing capital ₹3,50,000; liabilities ₹1,00,000.

topics.title: Grouping, marshalling, opening entry and preparing statements

learn.hook: A balance sheet with 60 random lines is hard to read. Grouping and marshalling arrange it like a well-organised kitchen: similar things together, and in a sensible order.
points: Grouping: putting similar items under a common head, e.g. cash in hand and cash at bank as 'Cash and cash equivalents'; sundry debtors under 'Trade receivables'.

Marshalling: arranging assets and liabilities in a particular order. Order of liquidity: assets from most liquid (cash, bank, debtors, stock) to least liquid (goodwill); liabilities from most urgent (bank overdraft, creditors) to capital.
Order of permanence: the reverse. Assets from most permanent (goodwill, land, building) to cash; liabilities from capital to current liabilities. Companies follow this broadly under Schedule III.
Opening entry at the start of a new year: Dr all assets / Cr all liabilities and capital, bringing forward last year's balance sheet.
Preparing statements from a trial balance (no adjustments): nominal items go to the trading and P&L account; real and personal items go to the balance sheet; net profit is added to capital.

example.q: On 1 April: cash ₹20,000, stock ₹50,000, furniture ₹30,000, creditors ₹25,000. Pass the opening entry.
steps: Dr Cash ₹20,000, Dr Stock ₹50,000, Dr Furniture ₹30,000 / Cr Creditors ₹25,000, Cr Capital ₹75,000.
example.answer: Dr Cash, Stock, Furniture (₹1,00,000) / Cr Creditors ₹25,000, Capital ₹75,000

learn.reallife: Balance sheets of Indian banks list cash and RBI balances first, close to the order of liquidity, while manufacturing companies like Tata Steel start with property, plant and equipment.

topics.title: Need for adjustments and the treatment of closing stock

learn.hook: The trial balance is a rough draft. Unpaid March salaries, next year's insurance paid today and unsold stock are all missing or misplaced. Adjustments turn the draft into a true picture.
points: Adjustments make the final accounts follow the accrual and matching concepts: every income and expense of the year, and only of the year, is included.

Golden rule: an item given INSIDE the trial balance appears at ONE place in the final accounts; an adjustment given OUTSIDE the trial balance appears at TWO places (double effect), e.g. P&L and balance sheet.
Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower (conservatism).
Closing stock given outside the trial balance: credit side of the trading account and current asset in the balance sheet.
Closing stock given inside the trial balance (with adjusted purchases, i.e. purchases already reduced by closing stock): shown only in the balance sheet, not in the trading account.

example.q: Closing stock: cost ₹90,000, net realisable value ₹84,000; given outside the trial balance. Show its treatment.
steps: Trading account credit side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
Balance sheet assets side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
example.answer: ₹84,000 on the credit of the trading account and as a current asset in the balance sheet.

topics.title: Outstanding and prepaid expenses

learn.hook: March salary is paid on 7 April. Next year's insurance is paid in January. Both payments land in the wrong year unless we adjust them.
points: Outstanding expense: incurred during the year but not yet paid. Adjusting entry: Dr Expense / Cr Outstanding Expense.
Treatment: add to the expense in the P&L (or trading) account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance for a period beyond the year. Adjusting entry: Dr Prepaid Expense / Cr Expense.
Treatment: deduct from the expense in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Outstanding wages go to the trading account (wages are direct); outstanding salaries, rent and so on go to the P&L account.

example.q: Rent paid during 2025-26 is ₹55,000 (11 months). Monthly rent ₹5,000. Insurance paid ₹12,000 on 1 October 2025 for one year. Show the adjustments.
steps: Rent outstanding = 1 month = ₹5,000; P&L rent = 55,000 + 5,000 = ₹60,000; liability ₹5,000.
Insurance: October to March = 6 months used; prepaid = 6/12 × 12,000 = ₹6,000.
example.answer: Rent ₹60,000 (outstanding ₹5,000 liability); insurance ₹6,000 (prepaid ₹6,000 asset).

learn.reallife: Indian companies show 'outstanding expenses' under other current liabilities and 'prepaid expenses' under other current assets in their Schedule III balance sheets.

topics.title: Accrued income and income received in advance

learn.hook: Your fixed deposit earned interest in March, but the bank credits it in April. You've earned it already. And a tenant who pays April's rent in March? You haven't earned that yet.
points: Accrued income: earned during the year but not yet received, e.g. interest accrued on investments, commission earned not received.
Adjusting entry: Dr Accrued Income / Cr Income. Treatment: add to the income in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Income received in advance (unearned income): received during the year for a service to be given next year, e.g. rent received in advance.
Adjusting entry: Dr Income / Cr Income Received in Advance. Treatment: deduct from the income in the P&L account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.

example.q: Investments ₹2,00,000 at 9% p.a.; interest received during the year ₹12,000. Rent received ₹60,000 includes ₹10,000 for the next year. Show the treatment.
steps: P&L: interest ₹18,000; balance sheet: accrued interest ₹6,000 (current asset).
Rent: P&L 60,000 − 10,000 = ₹50,000; balance sheet: rent received in advance ₹10,000 (current liability).
example.answer: Interest ₹18,000 (accrued ₹6,000 asset); rent ₹50,000 (₹10,000 advance as liability).

topics.title: Depreciation and bad debts as adjustments

learn.hook: A furniture showroom's balance sheet should not show three-year-old furniture at its original price, nor debtors who have vanished. Two adjustments fix that.
points: Depreciation adjustment: debit P&L account with depreciation; deduct it from the asset in the balance sheet.
If an asset is added during the year, depreciation on the addition is charged only for the months used (unless told otherwise).
Bad debts given inside the trial balance: debited to P&L only (debtors are already reduced).
Further bad debts given as an adjustment: add to bad debts in P&L, and deduct from debtors in the balance sheet.
Bad debts recovered (an amount written off earlier, now received) is credited to P&L as an income.

example.q: Machinery ₹3,00,000 (including ₹60,000 bought on 1 October 2025). Depreciation 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March 2026. Debtors ₹1,20,000; bad debts in trial balance ₹3,000; further bad debts ₹2,000. Show the treatment.
steps: Depreciation on ₹2,40,000 for 12 months = ₹24,000; on ₹60,000 for 6 months = ₹3,000; total ₹27,000.
P&L debit: depreciation ₹27,000; balance sheet: machinery 3,00,000 − 27,000 = ₹2,73,000.
Bad debts in P&L = 3,000 + 2,000 = ₹5,000; debtors in balance sheet = 1,20,000 − 2,000 = ₹1,18,000.
example.answer: Depreciation ₹27,000 (machinery ₹2,73,000); bad debts ₹5,000 (debtors ₹1,18,000).

topics.title: Provision for doubtful debts and provision for discount on debtors

learn.hook: First remove the debtors who won't pay at all, then the ones who might not, and finally the discount the good ones will take for paying early. The order matters.
points: Provision for doubtful debts (PDD) is calculated as a percentage of debtors after deducting further bad debts.
P&L charge = Bad debts (trial balance) + Further bad debts + New PDD − Old PDD. If the result is negative, the surplus is credited to P&L.
Balance sheet: Debtors − Further bad debts − New PDD.
Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts and the new PDD (only good debtors receive discount).
It is debited to P&L (less any old provision for discount) and deducted from debtors in the balance sheet.

example.q: Debtors ₹1,00,000; further bad debts ₹4,000; PDD 5%; provision for discount 2%. Old PDD ₹3,000; bad debts in TB ₹1,000. Find the P&L charges and net debtors.
steps: Debtors after bad debts = ₹96,000; new PDD = 5% = ₹4,800.
example.answer: P&L: ₹6,800 for bad and doubtful debts and ₹1,824 for discount; net debtors ₹89,376.

topics.title: Manager's commission

learn.hook: A store manager is promised 10% of profit. But 10% of which profit: before her commission is deducted, or after? The answer changes her pay.
points: Commission on net profit before charging such commission: Commission = Net profit (before commission) × Rate ÷ 100.
Commission on net profit after charging such commission: Commission = Net profit (before commission) × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate).
The second is smaller, because the base itself is reduced by the commission.
Commission is debited to the P&L account. If unpaid at the year-end, it is shown as outstanding commission, a current liability.

example.q: Net profit before commission ₹2,20,000. Manager's commission 10% (a) before charging commission, (b) after charging commission.

learn.reallife: Retail chains in India often reward store managers with a commission on store profit; contracts specify whether it is calculated before or after the commission itself.

topics.title: Interest on capital and interest on drawings

learn.hook: A proprietor who invests ₹10 lakh could have earned interest in a bank. Charging interest on capital shows whether the business earns more than that bank deposit would have.
points: Interest on capital: an expense of the business, debited to P&L; added to the owner's capital in the balance sheet. Entry: Dr Interest on Capital / Cr Capital.
Interest on drawings: an income of the business, credited to P&L; deducted from capital in the balance sheet (directly or through drawings). Entry: Dr Drawings (or Capital) / Cr Interest on Drawings.
Interest on capital = Capital × Rate × Time. If capital is added during the year, interest on the addition runs from the date of addition.
Interest on drawings = Drawings × Rate × Period for which the money was withdrawn.
These adjustments do not change the owner's final capital in total; they show the true earnings of the business.

example.q: Capital ₹5,00,000 on 1 April 2025; interest on capital 8% p.a. Drawings ₹40,000 withdrawn on 1 October 2025; interest on drawings 6% p.a. Year ends 31 March 2026.
steps: Interest on capital = 5,00,000 × 8% = ₹40,000 (debit P&L; add to capital).
Interest on drawings = 40,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,200 (credit P&L; deduct from capital).
example.answer: Interest on capital ₹40,000; interest on drawings ₹1,200.

learn.reallife: A family-run sweet shop in Agra might find that after charging 8% interest on the owner's capital, the business earns barely more than a bank FD, a useful reality check.

topics.title: Other adjustments: abnormal loss, goods withdrawn, samples, unrecorded items

learn.hook: A godown fire, a proprietor taking goods home and boxes given away as samples all reduce the goods available for sale. Each needs a careful two-place treatment.
points: Abnormal loss of goods (fire, theft, flood) given as an adjustment: credit the trading account with the full cost of goods lost; debit P&L with the loss not covered by insurance; show the insurance claim admitted as a current asset.
Goods withdrawn by the proprietor (adjustment): deduct from purchases in the trading account (at cost) and add to drawings (deducted from capital).
Goods distributed as free samples (adjustment): deduct from purchases and debit advertisement in P&L.
Unrecorded credit sales: add to sales and to debtors. Unrecorded credit purchases (goods included in stock): add to purchases and to creditors.
Goods sent on approval and wrongly recorded as sales, not yet approved: reduce sales and debtors by the sale price, and include them in closing stock at cost.

example.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 destroyed by fire; insurance claim admitted ₹30,000 (adjustment). Show the treatment.
steps: Trading account credit: Loss by fire (goods destroyed) ₹50,000.
Balance sheet assets: insurance claim receivable ₹30,000.
example.answer: Trading Cr ₹50,000; P&L Dr ₹20,000; balance sheet asset ₹30,000.

topics.title: Final accounts with multiple adjustments

learn.hook: This is the big question of the Class 11 exam: a trial balance with six or seven adjustments. Work methodically, one adjustment at a time, and the balance sheet will tally.
points: Work in order: closing stock; outstanding and prepaid expenses; accrued and advance incomes; depreciation; bad debts and provisions; manager's commission; interest on capital and drawings.
For each adjustment outside the trial balance, record both effects before moving on; tick it off.
Trading account first (gross profit), then P&L (net profit), then the balance sheet.
Capital in the balance sheet: Opening capital + Net profit + Interest on capital − Drawings − Interest on drawings.
If the balance sheet does not tally, check that each adjustment appears twice and each trial balance item once.

example.q: Gross profit ₹2,00,000. Salaries ₹60,000 (outstanding ₹6,000). Rent ₹24,000 (prepaid ₹2,000). Commission received ₹10,000 (accrued ₹2,000). Depreciation on furniture ₹50,000 at 10%. Find net profit.

chapters.title: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records

topics.title: Incomplete records: meaning and features

learn.hook: The paan shop near your school probably keeps a notebook of cash and a list of who owes money, and nothing else. That is accounting from incomplete records.
points: Incomplete records (often called the single entry system) are accounting records not kept strictly on the double entry system.
Usually only a cash book and personal accounts of debtors and creditors are kept; real accounts (assets) and nominal accounts (expenses, incomes) are generally not kept.
Features: no uniformity (methods differ from firm to firm); business and personal transactions are often mixed; heavy reliance on vouchers, memory and information from outside sources.
It is suited to small sole traders and partnership firms; companies cannot use it, because the law requires double entry books.

example.q: A small florist keeps a cash diary and a list of hotel customers who pay monthly. She does not record rent, wages or her shop fittings in any account. What kind of records are these?
steps: Only cash and personal (debtors) accounts are kept.
Nominal accounts (rent, wages) and real accounts (fittings) are missing.
So these are incomplete records, not a double entry system.
example.answer: Incomplete records (single entry).

learn.reallife: Many street vendors registered under PM SVANidhi keep only cash and dues records; as they grow, digital apps help them shift to complete books.

topics.title: Reasons for incomplete records and their limitations

learn.hook: Incomplete records are cheap and easy, like cooking without a recipe. But when the tax officer or the bank manager asks for proof, the shortcut becomes expensive.
points: Reasons: used by small traders with few transactions; owners lack accounting knowledge; low cost (no trained accountant needed); simple and less time-consuming.

Limitations: no trial balance, so arithmetical accuracy cannot be checked; true profit or loss is hard to find; a proper balance sheet cannot be prepared; not acceptable to tax authorities as complete books; banks hesitate to lend; frauds and errors are hard to detect; no control over assets.
Profit can still be estimated by comparing capital at two dates (the statement of affairs method).
The conversion method (rebuilding full double entry final accounts from incomplete records) is outside the CBSE Class 11 syllabus; only the statement of affairs method is studied.

example.q: A trader with incomplete records applies for a loan. Give two reasons the bank may hesitate.
steps: Without double entry books, his profit figure cannot be verified.
He cannot produce a reliable balance sheet showing assets and liabilities.
So the bank cannot judge his repaying capacity or the security.
example.answer: Profit cannot be verified and no reliable balance sheet exists.

learn.reallife: GST registration nudges many small Indian businesses to keep fuller records, because input tax credit needs proper invoices and books.

topics.title: Statement of affairs and finding capital

learn.hook: If you can't trace every transaction, take two photographs instead: one at the start of the year and one at the end. Each photograph of assets and liabilities is a statement of affairs.
points: A statement of affairs is a statement of all assets and liabilities on a date, prepared from incomplete records. The difference is the capital: Capital = Total assets − Total liabilities.
Format: like a balance sheet, liabilities and capital on the left, assets on the right; capital is the balancing figure.

Statement of affairs vs balance sheet: the statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records and values are often estimates; capital is a balancing figure; omissions are hard to detect. A balance sheet is prepared from a double entry ledger, values come from ledger balances, and capital is taken from the capital account.
Opening statement of affairs gives opening capital; closing statement of affairs gives closing capital.

example.q: On 1 April: cash ₹15,000, stock ₹60,000, debtors ₹45,000, furniture ₹30,000, creditors ₹40,000. On 31 March: cash ₹20,000, stock ₹75,000, debtors ₹55,000, furniture ₹27,000, creditors ₹47,000. Find opening and closing capital.
example.answer: Opening capital ₹1,10,000; closing capital ₹1,30,000.

topics.title: Finding profit by comparing capitals

learn.hook: If your piggy bank grew from ₹1,000 to ₹1,500, did you earn ₹500? Only if you didn't take money out or put extra in. Business profit works the same way.
points: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital.
Drawings are added back because they reduced closing capital but were not a loss of the business.
Additional capital is deducted because it increased closing capital but was not earned.
A negative result means a loss.

The formula can be rearranged to find any missing figure: Opening capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Profit; Drawings = Profit + Opening capital + Additional capital − Closing capital.

example.q: Opening capital ₹2,00,000; closing capital ₹2,60,000; drawings ₹30,000; additional capital ₹40,000. Find profit.

topics.title: Statement of profit or loss with adjustments

learn.hook: The capital-comparison profit is a rough figure. Before reporting it, an accountant charges interest on capital, adds interest on drawings and accounts for items like depreciation that the closing figures may have missed.
points: Statement of profit or loss format: Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital = Adjusted closing capital; less Opening capital = Profit before adjustments.

Then: Less interest on capital; add interest on drawings. Also adjust for depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, further bad debts, outstanding expenses (less) and accrued income or prepaid expenses (add), if they have not already been reflected in the closing statement of affairs.
Interest on capital is usually calculated on opening capital (and on additional capital from its date).
The final figure is the net profit (or loss) for the year.
Best practice: apply asset-related adjustments (depreciation, bad debts, provisions, outstanding items) while preparing the closing statement of affairs, so that closing capital is correct.

example.q: Profit before adjustments ₹60,000. Opening capital ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 5%. Interest on drawings ₹1,000. Find net profit.

learn.reallife: Chartered accountants in small towns often prepare such statements for traders' income tax returns, then advise them to keep complete books from the next year.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
